challenges.judge_assessment: This lands hard. The cited authority for the status issue points the other way: R.C. 5321.01 ties 'tenant' to a rental agreement, and the local authority the appellees rely on treats 5321.15 as a landlord-tenant remedy, not a free-standing right of a cohabitant or guest to stay in another person's home. On this record the brief never identifies a rental agreement, leasehold, or other statutory tenancy; it leans instead on 'consorts/house companions,' moving in at Edwin's request, and a power of attorney. The brief does not really answer the threshold problem. If the court accepts this attack, the lockout and Chapter 1923 arguments lose their statutory foundation.
challenges.suggested_response: The summary-judgment record, viewed in Alice’s favor, shows that she lived at Red Hill with Edwin’s permission, that Cathryn twice changed the locks and posted notices barring Alice from entering, and that Edwin later directed that Alice be removed. At minimum, those facts created a genuine issue whether appellees resorted to self-help and wrongfully prevented Alice from retrieving her property; summary judgment therefore could not be entered on the premise that appellees established, as a matter of law, the right to exclude her without judicial process.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: This paragraph needs either record support for a rental agreement or a different theory. On the record supplied, the brief cannot safely call Alice a tenant under R.C. 5321.01; if no tenancy evidence exists, the passage should be narrowed to the admitted lockouts and the factual dispute over appellees' conduct.

challenges.opponent_argument: Even on the brief's own account, the lock changes do not automatically become an unlawful self-help eviction unless Alice was within the class protected by the landlord-tenant statutes. Brown v. Ray reflects that R.C. 5321.15 is a lockout remedy in a landlord-tenant setting; it does not create a general right to remain in another person's home against the owner's direction. If Alice was a non-tenant cohabitant or licensee, changing the locks and posting notices is not the statutory violation the brief assumes it is.
challenges.why_it_matters: This defeats the core self-help theory: without protected tenant status, the lock-change allegations do not establish liability under the cited statutes.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is the same vulnerability from a different angle and it is also strong. The brief's self-help theory depends on Alice being within the class protected by the landlord-tenant statutes. The cited local authority specifically distinguishes ordinary owner-occupant/trespasser situations from landlord-tenant lockout cases. The brief tries to answer by calling Alice an occupant at will or sufferance and invoking Chapter 1923, but that only works if the status issue is resolved in her favor. Without that, changing the locks and posting notices is not automatically unlawful under the cited statutes.
challenges.suggested_response: Appellees did not establish, as a matter of law, that their repeated lock changes and exclusion of Alice were lawful. The record shows that Cathryn changed the locks and told Alice not to enter, and that Edwin later directed Alice’s removal; Alice’s affidavit further states that her personal property remained in the residence and was never returned. Those facts present a genuine issue whether appellees used self-help to dispossess Alice and retain her belongings without resort to judicial process.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Do not present R.C. 5321.15 as a free-standing lockout statute on this record. If the brief cannot show tenant status, it should remove the statute-specific conclusion and rely instead on the disputed facts showing repeated lock changes, notice-posting, and exclusion while Alice’s belongings remained inside.

That is not enough to carry conversion on summary judgment.
challenges.why_it_matters: Without proof tying particular property to Alice and showing wrongful dominion by appellees, the conversion claim cannot survive.

results.assessment: The brief reads credibly when it describes repeated lock changes, exclusion from the residence, and retention of Alice’s belongings, but its biggest weakness is that it never firmly establishes Alice as a tenant or otherwise protected occupant under the statutes it invokes. That gap undermines both the lockout/Chapter 1923 theory and the R.C. 5321.15 argument, because those claims depend on a status showing the brief does not squarely supply. The conversion claim is also thinly supported: it identifies categories of property and says appellees kept them, but the proof of ownership and dominion is generalized. The research does not rescue the status problem.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is a real vulnerability, but not a clean knockout. Ohio authority cited by the attack defines a tenant by reference to a rental agreement, and the brief does not identify any written lease or rental agreement. That said, the brief does not rest only on strict tenant status: it says Alice moved in at Edwin's request, was an occupant at his will or sufferance, and was still entitled to Chapter 1923 process before exclusion. On this record, the court could view the point as answered only in part; the advocate risks losing the 5321.15 framing if the court insists on statutory tenant status, but may still survive on the Chapter 1923 / unlawful detention theory.
challenges.suggested_response: Even if appellees contend the record does not establish Alice as a statutory tenant under R.C. 5321.01, the summary-judgment record still shows that she occupied the Red Hill residence with Edwin’s permission, was excluded by changed locks, and was directed to leave without any showing that appellees first resorted to the process provided by Chapter 1923. On this record, appellees were not entitled to judgment as a matter of law on the theory that they could simply use self-help to exclude Alice and detain her property.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Do not rest the lockout claim on R.C. 5321.15 unless the brief can actually point to a rental agreement in the record. Recast the point as an alternative Chapter 1923 unlawful-detention argument based on the evidence that Alice occupied the premises, was excluded by changed locks, and was told to leave without any shown resort to judicial process.

challenges.opponent_argument: The conversion claim is underdeveloped because the brief never shows the essential element of wrongful dominion. It says only that Alice left belongings in the residence and that the appellees kept them and did not return them. That is not enough, standing alone, to establish conversion. The authority the brief cites for conversion requires wrongful control or dominion inconsistent with the owner's rights, and the retrieved Ohio authority also points to the absence of conversion without demand and refusal. The brief does not identify any clear demand for return that was refused, nor any specific act showing dominion over the property beyond the disputed lockout.
challenges.why_it_matters: Without proof of wrongful dominion, the conversion claim fails as a matter of law, regardless of whether Alice had property in the house.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is the strongest merits attack against the conversion claim. The brief does say the items were left in the residence and never returned, and it says Alice repeatedly returned to recover them. That gives the appellant something to work with on demand and refusal. But the brief is thinner on the actual dominion element: it mostly relies on the lockout plus retention of belongings, without much developed authority showing that conduct alone is conversion. So the attack is not defeated, but it is not fatal either; it would land as a serious summary-judgment issue on the conversion count if the court thinks the facts stop short of wrongful dominion.
challenges.suggested_response: Alice averred that suits, dresses, craft materials, and personal papers remained in the residence, that appellees retained those items, and that the property was never returned. She also averred that she returned to recover her belongings but was again locked out. Those facts permit a reasonable inference that appellees exercised wrongful control over Alice’s property in a manner inconsistent with her rights, and they create a genuine issue of material fact on conversion.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Strengthen the conversion analysis by tying wrongful dominion to the repeated lockouts and appellees’ continued retention of Alice’s property after she attempted to retrieve it. Do not rely on the conclusion alone; state the facts that permit the inference.

challenges.opponent_argument: Even taking the brief at its highest level of generality, it argues only that there were disputes somewhere in the record. The court must find a genuine issue on an essential element, and the brief does not pin that down in a way that compels reversal.
challenges.why_it_matters: Without a clearly identified factual dispute on an essential element, the requested reversal is not justified.

The brief does tie some facts to the major theories—occupancy, lockout, exclusion, and retention of belongings—but it does not present a tight element-by-element summary for each claim. They did not do so. The record contains evidence that Alice occupied Red Hill, that appellees changed the locks and excluded her, and that appellees retained her personal property after she attempted to recover it. Those facts create genuine issues of material fact on the unlawful-exclusion and conversion claims, and summary judgment was therefore improper.

challenges.opponent_argument: The brief's own chronology is internally muddled on the facts that supposedly make the exclusion unlawful. It says Alice returned on February 21 and found notices dated "that very day of February 28," then says she returned the following day and the locks were changed again, and later says a notice to quit was issued on February 28 after the locks had already been changed. That sequence is not coherent on its face. Because the legality of the lock changes turns on when they occurred relative to any notice or process, the brief's inconsistent timeline undercuts its claim that the exclusion was plainly unlawful.

results.assessment: The brief has a workable narrative: Alice occupied the residence with permission, was locked out, and her property was retained, so the unlawful-exclusion theory and some summary-judgment framing do hold up. But it is vulnerable on the biggest legal point because it never clearly establishes a rental agreement or other statutory tenant status, which weakens the Chapter 5321/1923 path. The conversion discussion is also thin: it relies on retention after the lockout without fully developing wrongful dominion or a clean demand-and-refusal showing. The closing argument is too general and does not tightly track each essential element, though the record conflict about dates is more a drafting blemish than a fatal flaw.

challenges.opponent_argument: The negligence-per-se theory is overbroad as a matter of Ohio law. The rule the brief relies on applies a landlord’s statutory duties under R.C. 5321.04; it does not transform a former owner, after conveyance or foreclosure, into a continuing statutory tortfeasor. The source the brief itself leans on for Ohio landlord negligence per se makes that point: the duty runs against a landlord who is a party to the rental agreement, while Ohio authority recognizes that prior owners are divested of obligations when title transfers.
challenges.why_it_matters: If negligence per se cannot attach to Stark after it ceased to own the property, the brief’s principal liability theory fails.

challenges.judge_assessment: This lands hard. The cited Ohio negligence-per-se authority, as used in the brief, runs against a claim against a landlord who is a party to the rental relationship; the secondary Ohio source the court has here also says former owners are ordinarily divested of rights and obligations when title transfers absent some contrary law or agreement. The brief tries to recast the duty as a lead-hazard duty owed to later occupants, but it does not give controlling Ohio authority extending R.C. 5321.04 negligence per se past transfer/foreclosure. Stark stands to lose its cleanest merits defense if the court accepts this attack.
challenges.suggested_response: Appellants do not ask this Court to hold that a former owner remains a landlord forever after title passes. The Third Party Complaint alleges that Stark was the owner when the City inspected the property, issued the lead-hazard control order, and set a deadline for compliance, and that Stark failed to comply before transferring the property. That alleged failure to obey the order and abate the known hazard is the operative wrongful conduct. At minimum, the complaint pleads a statutory and ordinance-based duty that existed while Stark controlled the premises, together with a breach that preceded the transfer and proximately caused Appellants’ injuries.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Narrow the negligence-per-se argument so it does not claim that Stark remained a statutory landlord after transfer. Focus instead on Stark’s alleged violation while it still owned the property: the City’s abatement order, Stark’s notice of the hazard, and Stark’s failure to comply before the transfer.

challenges.opponent_argument: The nuisance theory does not save the complaint. The brief asks this Court to adopt a continuing-liability rule for a former owner after transfer, but Ohio law does not recognize that former owners retain obligations to the property after title passes. The authorities the brief cites from other jurisdictions and the Restatement cannot override the Ohio rule that, absent a contrary agreement or law, the prior owner is divested of all rights and obligations when the property transfers.
challenges.why_it_matters: This defeats the attempt to keep liability alive after Stark no longer owned or controlled the premises.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is a real threat to the nuisance theory. The brief’s Restatement sections are persuasive only if Ohio is willing to adopt them in this setting, and the Ohio source supplied here points the other way by treating prior owners as divested when title passes. The brief does answer with a long nuisance section, but it does not produce controlling Ohio authority that a former owner of lead-contaminated housing remains liable after transfer until abatement. Stark could lose the main common-law backstop if the court rejects the Restatement extension.
challenges.suggested_response: The nuisance allegations are not an attempt to impose liability on Stark merely because it once owned the property. Appellants alleged that Stark knew of the lead hazard, received an order to correct it, failed to abate it, and left the condition in place before transferring the premises. Those allegations describe Stark’s own creation and maintenance of a dangerous condition while it was in control of the property. The later transfer does not erase the pleaded wrongful conduct or the harm alleged to have flowed from it. At minimum, the complaint states a claim that should not have been dismissed on the pleadings.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Do not rely on Restatement sections and out-of-state nuisance cases as if Ohio had adopted a continuing-liability rule. Instead, recast the nuisance theory as describing Stark’s own creation and maintenance of the hazardous condition before transfer, and make clear that the claim is based on Stark’s failure to abate while it still owned the property.

challenges.opponent_argument: The Third Party Complaint still fails because it does not allege a viable duty at the time of injury. The pleaded facts show, at most, that Stark once owned the property, received notice, and later transferred it. But Ohio law ties negligence-per-se and landlord duties to the landlord relationship, and a former owner is not a landlord simply because it once held title. Without a legally cognizable duty at the time Ashoura Carter was injured, the complaint does not state a claim.
challenges.why_it_matters: This is the cleanest ground for affirming dismissal regardless of any disputed facts about the sale or foreclosure.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is essentially the same core merits problem framed as pleading sufficiency. If the law does not recognize a duty owed by Stark after it ceased owning the property, the complaint fails no matter how many facts are accepted as true. The brief does plead notice, nondisclosure, and injury, but it does not solve the temporal duty problem on controlling Ohio authority. Stark stands to preserve the dismissal if the court accepts this framing.
challenges.suggested_response: The Third Party Complaint alleges more than a bare assertion that Stark once held title. It alleges that Stark knew of the lead hazard, was ordered by the City to correct it, failed to comply, and sold the property without abating the condition. Those allegations, accepted as true at the pleading stage, identify a legal duty arising from Stark’s ownership and control of the premises and its receipt of the abatement order, together with a breach that occurred before the transfer. Appellants were not required to prove that theory in their complaint; they were required only to plead facts that, if proven, would entitle them to relief. The complaint does so.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Answer the duty challenge by pleading duty from Stark’s status and conduct while it owned the property, not from a generalized claim that every former owner owes a continuing duty at the time of injury. Emphasize that the complaint alleges Stark received notice, was ordered to abate, and breached that order before the transfer.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is a plausible affirmance route, but it is not airtight on the record as presented. The cited Ohio material can support the notion that a former owner’s obligations end on transfer, which makes the conversion/56(F) complaint look less outcome-determinative. But the brief already squarely says Stark attached discovery responses, the court used extra-pleading facts, and the discovery request was ignored. So the attack is answerable, not fatal: Stark can argue any procedural error was harmless because the legal claim fails anyway, but that depends on the court accepting the underlying no-duty premise.
challenges.suggested_response: Stark’s motion did not rest on the four corners of the pleadings. It quoted from and relied on discovery responses, and the trial court then went further and resolved an extra-pleading factual question—whether Stark relinquished the premises through foreclosure rather than a direct sale—to support dismissal. Once the court relied on matters outside the pleadings, Appellants were entitled to the protections of Civ.R. 56, including an opportunity for discovery under Civ.R. 56(F), before judgment was entered. The error was prejudicial because the very fact the court used to dispose of the case was not alleged in the pleadings and was the subject of Appellants’ requested discovery.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Keep the procedural issue, but tie it to prejudice: the trial court used extra-pleading facts to supply the foreclosure premise that drove dismissal, and Appellants were entitled to discovery before any summary-judgment-type ruling. Do not concede harmlessness; instead, explain that the challenged facts were material to the court’s legal conclusion and were not properly resolved on a Rule 12(B)(6) motion.

attacks_proposed.argument: Even if Stark’s motion referenced discovery responses, that does not help the Carters on this appeal because the dispositive issue is legal, not factual: under Ohio landlord-tenant law, a prior owner’s obligations end when title transfers unless some separate agreement or law says otherwise. The brief’s requested discovery about Stark’s motives or financial interest could not create a continuing post-transfer duty where Ohio law says former owners are divested of their rights and obligations on transfer. So any error in not converting the motion or delaying for discovery was, at most, harmless.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: This takes the wind out of the Rule 56(F) theory and preserves the dismissal even if the trial court looked beyond the pleadings.

attacks_proposed.argument: The negligence-per-se theory is overbroad as a matter of Ohio law. The rule the brief relies on applies a landlord’s statutory duties under R.C. 5321.04; it does not transform a former owner, after conveyance or foreclosure, into a continuing statutory tortfeasor. The source the brief itself leans on for Ohio landlord negligence per se makes that point: the duty runs against a landlord who is a party to the rental agreement, while Ohio authority recognizes that prior owners are divested of obligations when title transfers.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If negligence per se cannot attach to Stark after it ceased to own the property, the brief’s principal liability theory fails.

attacks_proposed.argument: The nuisance theory does not save the complaint. The brief asks this Court to adopt a continuing-liability rule for a former owner after transfer, but Ohio law does not recognize that former owners retain obligations to the property after title passes. The authorities the brief cites from other jurisdictions and the Restatement cannot override the Ohio rule that, absent a contrary agreement or law, the prior owner is divested of all rights and obligations when the property transfers.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: This defeats the attempt to keep liability alive after Stark no longer owned or controlled the premises.

attacks_proposed.argument: The Third Party Complaint still fails because it does not allege a viable duty at the time of injury. The pleaded facts show, at most, that Stark once owned the property, received notice, and later transferred it. But Ohio law ties negligence-per-se and landlord duties to the landlord relationship, and a former owner is not a landlord simply because it once held title. Without a legally cognizable duty at the time Ashoura Carter was injured, the complaint does not state a claim.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: This is the cleanest ground for affirming dismissal regardless of any disputed facts about the sale or foreclosure.

attacks_proposed.argument: Causation is also not adequately pled against Stark. Ohio law still requires proximate cause, and the brief cannot satisfy that element by pointing only to Stark’s earlier ownership and a later similar lead-hazard order against a different owner. The passage of title and intervening ownership break the chain the brief asks the Court to assume. At minimum, the complaint’s causal theory is too speculative to attribute the later injury to Stark as a matter of law.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If causation is not plausibly tied to Stark’s conduct, the negligence claim fails even apart from the duty problem.

judge_assessments.assessment: This lands hard. The cited Ohio negligence-per-se authority, as used in the brief, runs against a claim against a landlord who is a party to the rental relationship; the secondary Ohio source the court has here also says former owners are ordinarily divested of rights and obligations when title transfers absent some contrary law or agreement. The brief tries to recast the duty as a lead-hazard duty owed to later occupants, but it does not give controlling Ohio authority extending R.C. 5321.04 negligence per se past transfer/foreclosure. Stark stands to lose its cleanest merits defense if the court accepts this attack.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: It says C.C.O. 240.04(e), R.C. 5321.04, and R.C. 3742.38 support negligence per se and a duty to future occupants, even after relinquishing title.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Ohio authority specifically addressing whether R.C. 5321.04 or the lead statutes impose a continuing duty on a former owner after transfer or foreclosure.

judge_assessments.assessment: This is a real threat to the nuisance theory. The brief’s Restatement sections are persuasive only if Ohio is willing to adopt them in this setting, and the Ohio source supplied here points the other way by treating prior owners as divested when title passes. The brief does answer with a long nuisance section, but it does not produce controlling Ohio authority that a former owner of lead-contaminated housing remains liable after transfer until abatement. Stark could lose the main common-law backstop if the court rejects the Restatement extension.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: It relies on Restatement (Second) of Torts §§ 840A and 373, plus out-of-state nuisance cases, to argue liability survives transfer until the hazard is abated.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Whether any Ohio appellate or Supreme Court decision has adopted Restatement §§ 840A or 373 for a former owner after conveyance, especially in a lead-hazard case.

judge_assessments.coverageNote: Ohio authority on whether a former owner can owe a tort duty to later occupants after foreclosure or sale, independent of current landlord status.

The cited Ohio material can support the notion that a former owner’s obligations end on transfer, which makes the conversion/56(F) complaint look less outcome-determinative. But the brief already squarely says Stark attached discovery responses, the court used extra-pleading facts, and the discovery request was ignored. So the attack is answerable, not fatal: Stark can argue any procedural error was harmless because the legal claim fails anyway, but that depends on the court accepting the underlying no-duty premise.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: It says Stark attached and quoted discovery responses, the motion should have been treated as summary judgment, and the court should have ruled on the Rule 56(F) request before dismissing.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: A binding Ohio case on whether attaching discovery responses to a dismissal motion requires conversion, and whether harmless-error review applies when the merits allegedly fail as a matter of law.

judge_assessments.assessment: This does not land as a pleading attack on this record. The brief expressly says causation allegations must be accepted as true at the dismissal stage and then argues the pleaded facts plus inferences are enough to get past Civ.R. 12(B)(6). The proposed attack reads like a summary-judgment argument about proof, not a Rule 12(B)(6) argument about sufficiency of allegations. The advocate would lose little because the court should not reach it at this stage.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: It says the complaint alleged Stark’s failure to warn, remove, or cover the lead hazard caused the child’s injuries, and that causation can be inferred or decided by a factfinder later.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Nothing further unless the court converts the case to summary judgment and looks for evidentiary proof of causation.

judge_assessments.assessment: This attack misfires. It criticizes the brief for not proving specific duration of the condition, but the case is being tested on a Civ.R. 12(B)(6) posture, where pleaded facts are taken as true and evidence is not required. The brief already recites the pleaded allegations about notice and the condition; the attack adds nothing the court should use here.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: It pleads the hazardous condition, Stark’s notice, and the City’s orders; the argument is framed around accepting those allegations as true.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Only relevant if the court converts to summary judgment and requires proof of duration rather than pleading allegations.

judge_assessments.assessment: Same problem as r6. The lack of an evidentiary excerpt of notice is not a ground to affirm a Civ.R. 12(B)(6) dismissal when the complaint pleads notice and the motion was allegedly supported by extra-pleading materials. The brief already says Stark had notice from a city inspection and orders to correct the hazard, so the attack does not identify a pleading defect the court would reach on this record.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: It alleges Stark was on notice after the city inspection and received notices and orders to correct the lead condition.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Would matter only on a converted summary-judgment record with a developed evidentiary dispute about notice.

results.verdict: not yet persuasive on the central post-transfer duty issue
results.assessment: The brief has its best footing in the pleading and procedure points: it alleges Stark knew of the hazard, received an abatement order, and failed to comply before transfer, and it plausibly argues the court relied on extra-pleading material without Civ.R. 56 protections. But the brief remains exposed on the main merits question, because the challenges identify a serious Ohio-law problem with treating a former owner as still liable after title passes. The negligence-per-se and nuisance theories both depend on extending duty beyond ownership, and the brief does not supply controlling Ohio authority doing that. Research also did not resolve any stronger post-transfer duty theory in the brief’s favor.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is the core vulnerability. The cited Ohio authority the attack relies on points to the general rule that ownership-transfer divests a prior owner of the property’s obligations unless some contrary legal relationship exists, while the brief’s negligence theory depends on Stark owing a continuing duty after it no longer held title or possession. The brief tries to answer by invoking the abatement order, the alleged pre-transfer notice, and general negligence principles, but it never cites a controlling Ohio case squarely imposing a post-transfer duty on a former owner in this setting. If the court accepts the attack, both the common-law negligence claim and much of the statutory theory fail at the threshold.
challenges.suggested_response: The Third Party Complaint states a claim because it alleges that Stark received the City’s February 2, 2005 lead-hazard control order while it still owned the premises, obtained an extension to comply, and nevertheless failed to abate the hazard before the property was transferred. Those allegations plead Stark’s own breach while it was subject to the order and in control of the premises. Although Ohio law generally provides that prior owners are divested of the property’s obligations upon transfer absent contrary law, see Steele v. McNatt, 102 Ohio App.3d 558, 562, 657 N.E.2d 575 (8th Dist. 1995), this case is about Stark’s failure to comply with an abatement order before relinquishing title, not liability based on ownership alone.

The brief’s own theory depends on treating Stark as perpetually responsible despite foreclosure or sale, which the cited Ohio law does not support.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If there was no legally cognizable duty when the injury occurred, the common-law negligence theory and the statutory negligence-per-se theory both fail at the threshold.

attacks_proposed.argument: The nuisance theory cannot carry the appeal because the brief relies on Restatement sections and out-of-state nuisance cases, but Ohio authority cited in the retrieved materials points the other way: predecessor owners are generally divested of liability when title transfers, absent continuing control or some contrary legal relationship. The brief’s own cited support does not establish that Ohio has adopted Restatement § 840A for a former owner who relinquished the premises through foreclosure or sale.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If Ohio does not recognize continuing nuisance liability for a former owner in these circumstances, the common-law nuisance claim drops out entirely.

attacks_proposed.argument: The causation showing is too attenuated. The brief’s own allegations are collective and generalized: it says the injuries were caused by the negligence of multiple defendants and later notes that the current owner also received a similar lead-hazard order (u223, u227). That is not the same as alleging facts tying Ashoura Carter’s injury to Stark’s specific omission. The cited authority still requires proximate cause, and the pleading does not identify why Stark, rather than later owners or other conditions, was the factual cause of the poisoning.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Without a plausible Stark-specific causal link, the dismissal can be affirmed even if some other defendant might have had a viable claim.

attacks_proposed.argument: The 56(F) complaint does not save the appeal. Even if the motion referenced discovery responses, the dispositive defect is substantive, not evidentiary: the cited Ohio materials frame these claims as landlord-duty claims, and the retrieved authority says prior owners generally lose the property’s obligations on transfer. Extra discovery cannot create a duty where Ohio law does not recognize one. So any failure to delay the ruling for discovery was, at most, harmless.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If discovery could not cure the missing duty, the asserted procedural error does not warrant reversal.

attacks_proposed.argument: The brief repeatedly asks the Court to recognize a new rule that a former owner remains liable after relinquishing title because the property once had lead hazards. But the retrieved Ohio authority already supplies the relevant framework: landlord duties attach to the landlord relationship, and former owners are ordinarily divested of the property’s obligations on transfer. Framing this as an “issue of first impression” does not overcome the fact that the requested rule would expand Ohio tort law beyond the cited statutory and common-law limits.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If the Court views this as an invitation to create new liability rather than apply existing law, the appeal becomes much harder to win.

attacks_proposed.argument: The negligence-per-se theory still misses the key limiting element: the cited code and statute provisions impose duties on the owner/landlord who is subject to the order, not on a former owner after title has passed. The brief never supplies Ohio authority extending Cleveland’s lead-hazard order or R.C. 3742.37 to impose a continuing damages duty on someone who no longer owned or controlled the premises. Without that legal bridge, the asserted ordinance and statutory violations do not state a claim against Stark.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If the duty does not run to a former owner, the whole negligence-per-se theory collapses regardless of the severity of the alleged injury.

attacks_proposed.argument: The common-law nuisance theory also overreads the Restatement. The cited nuisance sections speak to a vendor or lessor who created or negligently allowed a nuisance to remain, but the brief’s own facts say Stark later sold the property and that a new owner then received a similar lead order. That sequence undercuts any claim that Stark remained responsible for a continuing nuisance after transfer, particularly where Ohio authority in the retrieved materials emphasizes that prior ownership alone does not preserve liability.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If the nuisance is treated as the later owner’s problem after transfer, Stark is out as a matter of law.

attacks_proposed.argument: The brief’s burden-shifting and inference arguments go too far. The cited Restatement discussion presupposes proof that each defendant engaged in tortious conduct and that one or more caused the harm; it does not let a plaintiff bypass the need to connect Stark’s own conduct to the injury. Here, the pleading simply lumps together multiple defendants, multiple transfers, and a later abatement order, which makes the proposed inference of Stark-specific causation speculative rather than reasonable.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If the Court rejects the proposed inference as speculation, the causation theory fails even under a generous pleading or summary-judgment lens.

judge_assessments.assessment: This is the core vulnerability. The cited Ohio authority the attack relies on points to the general rule that ownership-transfer divests a prior owner of the property’s obligations unless some contrary legal relationship exists, while the brief’s negligence theory depends on Stark owing a continuing duty after it no longer held title or possession. The brief tries to answer by invoking the abatement order, the alleged pre-transfer notice, and general negligence principles, but it never cites a controlling Ohio case squarely imposing a post-transfer duty on a former owner in this setting. If the court accepts the attack, both the common-law negligence claim and much of the statutory theory fail at the threshold.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: Stark allegedly knew of the lead hazard, received orders to remediate, and breached a non-delegable duty to future occupants by abandoning the property rather than fixing the hazard.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: A controlling Ohio case on whether a former landlord/owner retains a duty to later occupants after foreclosure or sale would resolve this.

judge_assessments.assessment: This lands substantially. The brief’s negligence-per-se theory depends on the proposition that Cleveland’s lead-hazard order and the cited statutes impose an enforceable duty on Stark even after it relinquished the property. The cited provisions, however, are framed in terms of the owner/landlord subject to the order, and the brief does not supply Ohio authority extending that duty to a former owner after transfer. The brief does say Stark was ordered to abate while it still owned the property, which is its best answer, but that only addresses notice and timing, not whether liability for damages survives once title passed.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief says Stark received a lead-hazard control order, got an extension, failed to abate, and that this statutory/ordinance violation is negligence per se.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Ohio authority on whether R.C. 3742.37/Cleveland lead-order duties create damages liability against a former owner after transfer would settle it.

judge_assessments.assessment: The nuisance theory is vulnerable. The brief relies on Restatement §§ 840A and 373 plus out-of-state nuisance cases, but the Ohio materials retrieved for the record do not show Ohio adopting continuing nuisance liability for a former owner who has transferred the land, especially not in a foreclosure/sale posture. The brief does answer with DiCenzo and the general proposition that Ohio courts look to the Restatement, but that is not the same as Ohio adopting the specific predecessor-liability rule the brief needs. On this record, the court could well treat this as an unsupported attempt to extend Ohio nuisance law.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief argues a vendor or lessor who created or allowed a nuisance to remain can remain liable after transfer and cites Restatement §§ 840A and 373, plus DiCenzo.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: An Ohio decision adopting or rejecting Restatement § 840A for former owners would control this point.

judge_assessments.assessment: This is the fact-specific version of the nuisance attack. The record does show the brief’s own allegations that Stark later sold the property and a later owner also received a lead order, which makes the continuing-nuisance theory harder to sustain as to Stark. But the Restatement language the brief quotes is not limited to current owners; it expressly contemplates liability after transfer if the vendor created or negligently permitted the nuisance to remain. The brief already makes that response. So this is a real weakness, but not a clean knock-out on the present record.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief says transfer does not automatically end liability and that a vendor who created or allowed a nuisance to persist remains responsible under Restatement principles.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Ohio authority on whether a lead hazard qualifies as a continuing nuisance after transfer would settle the issue.

judge_assessments.assessment: This attack is weaker than the duty attacks because the brief’s pleading-stage theory does not need to prove source causation in full. The complaint alleges Stark knew of the hazard, failed to remediate it, and that the child suffered lead poisoning while the premises remained hazardous. The opponent is right that the allegations are collective and that a later owner also appears in the story, which makes Stark-specific causation less clean. But the brief already answers that causation may be inferred at this stage and need not be proven yet. On this record, the court is unlikely to affirm solely on this point if it is applying a pleading standard.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief says the pleadings allege Stark’s failure to remediate contributed to the child’s lead poisoning and that causation can be inferred or left for the jury.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Evidence tying the child’s exposure period and source to Stark’s ownership, rather than later owners or later conditions, would settle this.

judge_assessments.assessment: This procedural attack has some force only if the court agrees the motion actually relied on materials outside the pleadings and that the trial court should have converted the motion or deferred for Civ.R. 56(F) discovery. The brief expressly says it made that argument below and that the court ignored the 56(F) request. But the attack’s harmless-error theory depends on the substantive duty question being already foreclosed; that is not established on this record. So while the opponent can argue discovery would not create a duty, the court could still view the failure to address conversion/56(F) as reversible if extra-pleading materials drove the dismissal.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief says Stark quoted and attached discovery responses, the Carters sought Rule 56(F) discovery, and the trial court dismissed under Rule 12(B)(6) without addressing those issues.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The journal entry and record citations on whether the court relied on materials outside the pleadings, and whether the 56(F) request was preserved, would settle this.

judge_assessments.assessment: This is mostly an extension of the causation attack and is only partially persuasive here. The cited burden-shifting discussion presupposes multiple tortfeasors and uncertainty over which actor caused the harm, but the brief uses it to argue that Stark-specific causation can be inferred from a collective factual narrative. The opponent is right that the allegations are not tightly Stark-specific, yet the brief does allege Stark’s own notice, nonremediation, and abandonment of the property. That is enough to make this a contestable inference argument, not a clear basis for affirmance on this record.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief says multiple actors may share causal responsibility and that reasonable inferences on causation are for the jury when the facts support them.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Whether the complaint identifies Stark’s own tortious conduct with enough specificity, or merely lumps it together with other defendants, would settle this.

judge_assessments.assessment: This is more rhetoric than a dispositive legal attack. Saying the brief asks the court to create a new rule does not by itself answer whether the cited statutes, ordinances, or Restatement principles already support the claims. The brief openly frames the issue as one of first impression and then argues existing Ohio and Restatement authority supports liability. A court would not affirm simply because the requested result is novel; it would reach the actual duty and nuisance questions instead. So this point does not independently land on this record.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief says the appeal presents an issue of first impression and that Ohio law should recognize liability for a former owner who fails to remediate known lead hazards before relinquishing the property.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: No further research needed; the point is doctrinal framing, not a separate legal defect.

results.verdict: not yet persuasive on the central duty and liability theorie
results.assessment: The brief has a workable pleading-stage causation story and a decent answer on timing and discovery, but it is exposed where the appeal most depends on Ohio law: it never squarely shows a continuing duty for Stark after transfer, and it lacks Ohio authority extending the lead-hazard order and negligence-per-se statutes to a former owner. The nuisance theory is also shaky because it leans on Restatement and out-of-state authority without showing Ohio has adopted the specific predecessor-liability rule needed here. The causation arguments are weaker than the duty attacks and probably not enough by themselves to save the case, but they are not the main problem. The research did not settle a clean Ohio rule that fills the post-transfer duty gap.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is a real point, but it does not cleanly defeat the brief. The authorities actually cited in the brief for this section are the appellate rules and the court’s own order, and a court in Ohio does have discretion to impose dismissal or other sanctions for failure to perfect the record or obey an appellate order. results.assessment: The brief has solid points where it ties relief to the existing record: the nonpayment finding, the trial court’s express burden finding, and the request to disregard extra-record materials. But it overreaches in two places that need fixing. First, the dismissal request is too absolute; the cited record problems support exclusion or other sanctions more naturally than automatic dismissal. Second, the merits language is too categorical in saying repair issues cannot be a defense absent escrow, because the research shows repair-related defenses and setoff concepts exist in Ohio law. The scope-of-relief point is also overstated to the extent it suggests blanket striking rather than selective exclusion.

challenges.judge_assessment: This lands as a real merits attack because the brief states the rule too categorically: it says a tenant cannot use the condition of the premises or failure to repair as a defense unless rent was escrowed. The cited Ohio materials do not read that broadly. The brief’s own authorities, Smith and Martins Ferry, do support excluding a repair-defense where the tenant was not current and did not escrow rent, and the record facts here say exactly that. But the additional sources the attacker points to recognize other repair-related theories, so the appellee’s framing is vulnerable if appellant actually preserved a different defense such as setoff or a repair agreement. On this record, though, the brief already answers most of the point by saying the only defense raised was repairs and no escrow was ever made. The advocate stands to lose the categorical formulation, not necessarily the affirmance.
challenges.suggested_response: Appellee does not contend that every repair-related theory is foreclosed in every case. On this record, however, the only defense Ealy raised was the landlord’s alleged failure to make repairs, and the record shows that Ealy and his wife did not deposit rent in escrow under R.C. 5321.07 or otherwise pursue a rent-deposit remedy. In these circumstances, and under Smith v. Wright and Martins Ferry Jaycee Housing, Inc. v. Pawlaczyk, the condition of the premises was not a valid defense to STJ’s action for restitution.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Narrow the escrow point so it does not read as a categorical rule against every repair-related theory. Acknowledge that Ohio materials recognize other repair-related doctrines in some settings, but emphasize that none is shown on this record and that Ealy did not escrow rent or otherwise preserve a repair-based defense here.

challenges.opponent_argument: The request for dismissal or striking the brief is overreaching. The brief identifies alleged violations of App.R. 9(B), 13(B), and 16, but it does not cite any authority showing that those defects automatically require the extreme sanction of dismissal or striking the entire appeal. On the brief's own showing, the court is asked to leap from procedural noncompliance to the harshest possible remedy without explaining why a narrower response would not suffice.
challenges.why_it_matters: If the court rejects the sanction request as overbroad, the appeal survives and the merits must be reached.

The rules and the order are real, and the brief alleges concrete noncompliance, so the problem is not the factual predicate; it is the missing sanction standard. challenges.judge_assessment: This lands on the hardest legal step in the brief: even if § 3617 reaches retaliatory nonrenewal, the brief still has to show that federal law gives Masten a defense to possession in a forcible-entry-and-detainer case. The cited federal cases support retaliation claims and, in some jurisdictions, a defense to possession, but the Ohio authorities the brief itself cites treat holdover possession as a separate statutory remedy. The brief does answer with Matarese and similar cases, but not with Ohio authority squarely saying § 3617 defeats eviction after lease expiration on this record.
challenges.suggested_response: Section 3617 does not merely create a damages claim; it makes it unlawful to coerce, intimidate, threaten, or interfere with a person because that person exercised or assisted another in exercising protected fair-housing rights. Where the eviction itself is alleged to be the retaliatory act, the question is whether the landlord may use possession proceedings to accomplish what federal law forbids. The authorities cited by Appellant, including Matarese and the FHA’s anti-interference provisions, support the conclusion that retaliatory nonrenewal based on protected fair-housing activity may be raised as a defense to eviction, and § 3615 confirms that state law may not be applied to permit conduct the FHA makes unlawful.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Concede the doctrinal distinction that § 3617 does not itself grant possession, then argue the federal Fair Housing Act still makes retaliatory nonrenewal a defense to eviction when the tenant is asserting protected fair-housing rights. If you cannot support that defense with Ohio authority, say so expressly and rely on the federal cases and § 3615 as the best available authority.

challenges.opponent_argument: The absence of the R.C. 5321.03(A)(4) language from Chapter 4112 does not prove that a holdover tenant may assert a retaliatory-eviction defense under the Ohio Fair Housing Act. The relevant question is whether Ohio law recognizes a Chapter 4112 possession defense that overrides the landlord's right to recover from a holdover tenant; the supplied authorities do not. Indian Hills and the holdover exception address the possession remedy itself, not just the wording of Chapter 5321.
challenges.why_it_matters: This defeats the claimed statutory distinction on which the Chapter 4112 argument depends.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is a real vulnerability. The brief's distinction is that Chapter 4112 lacks the holdover-tenant language found in R.C. 5321.03(A)(4), so Indian Hills should not be imported. But the cited materials do not supply a case saying Chapter 4112 creates a possession defense that overrides the landlord's holdover-rights rule. The brief tries to bridge that gap by analogizing to federal FHA cases and Ohio courts' use of federal guidance, yet the statutory-translation step remains underdeveloped.
challenges.suggested_response: Chapter 4112 is a fair-housing statute, not a landlord-tenant holdover provision. The absence of the specific R.C. 5321.03(A)(4) holdover language from Chapter 4112 is one reason the Trial Court should not have imported Indian Hills into this case; Ohio courts construe Chapter 4112 in light of analogous federal fair-housing law, and that law does not permit a court to use a holdover rule to defeat a bona fide fair-housing retaliation defense without authority saying Chapter 4112 requires that result.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Do not overstate the Chapter 4112 point as a textual-one-to-one comparison with R.C. 5321.03(A)(4). Instead, say Ohio courts look to federal fair-housing precedent when construing Chapter 4112, and because Chapter 4112 is a fair-housing statute rather than the landlord-tenant holdover statute, Indian Hills should not be imported wholesale without authority.

challenges.opponent_argument: The Supremacy Clause point overreaches. The brief identifies no Ohio or federal authority showing that the Fair Housing Act requires Ohio courts to ignore the holdover-tenant rule in a forcible-entry-and-detainer case. The Ohio materials supplied here recognize that rule as a valid limit on the retaliation defense, so there is no demonstrated actual conflict to preempt.
challenges.why_it_matters: If there is no genuine conflict, the trial court was not required to discard the Ohio eviction rule.

challenges.judge_assessment: The preemption/Supremacy Clause point is only as strong as the showing of conflict, and the brief does not make that showing cleanly. The cited federal authorities support the general proposition that conflicting state law yields, and § 3615 can invalidate state law that permits discriminatory housing practices. But the brief still has to demonstrate that Indian Hills, as applied here, actually conflicts with federal law rather than simply coexisting with a landlord's holdover remedy. The brief gestures at that conflict, but the record presented here leaves room for the opponent's narrower reading.
challenges.suggested_response: The issue is not whether Ohio courts must disregard state law in the abstract. The issue is whether a state rule may be applied to defeat enforcement of federal fair-housing rights. Under the Supremacy Clause, state law must give way to the extent it conflicts with federal law, and 42 U.S.C. § 3615 expressly provides that any state law that purports to require or permit conduct that would be a discriminatory housing practice is invalid to that extent. Applied here, Indian Hills cannot be used to extinguish Appellant’s federal fair-housing defense to possession.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Narrow the Supremacy Clause argument to an as-applied conflict: the court need not say all Ohio landlord-tenant law yields, only that it cannot use Indian Hills to bar a federally protected fair-housing defense. Tie the conflict directly to 42 U.S.C. § 3615 and the FHA’s prohibition on discriminatory housing practices.

challenges.suggested_response: Indian Hills should not be extended to a case alleging retaliation for protected fair-housing activity. A rule that allows a landlord to punish protected activity by nonrenewal and then invoke the resulting holdover status to foreclose any defense would chill reporting and assistance in housing-discrimination cases and undermine the public policy embodied in the Fair Housing Act and Chapter 4112. At a minimum, this Court should decline to extend Indian Hills beyond its own statutory context.

results.assessment: The brief reads strongest on causation: it does more than rely on timing and does cite protected activity, landlord knowledge, close nonrenewal, and an OCRC probable-cause finding, which helps create a fact issue. challenges.judge_assessment: This is the strongest attack on the brief’s merits. The record does show circumstantial evidence of retaliation—assistance to Thompson, Masten’s own charge, K&D’s knowledge, then nonrenewal and eviction—but the brief still relies heavily on timing and the OCRC probable-cause finding rather than direct proof that the nonrenewal was because of protected activity. Ohio retaliation authorities cited in the source materials treat proof and causation as factual questions, not presumptions. So the attack does not defeat the theory outright, but it meaningfully presses the brief’s weakest link on summary judgment.
challenges.suggested_response: Retaliation may be proved by circumstantial as well as direct evidence, and the tenant need only establish a causal connection by a preponderance of the evidence. The sequence here supports that inference: K&D learned that Ms. Masten had engaged in protected fair-housing activity, and thereafter issued the 81-day notice of nonrenewal and pursued eviction. At summary judgment, that evidence was more than enough to create a genuine issue of material fact as to motive; the court was not permitted to resolve that factual dispute in K&D’s favor. The record therefore supports, at minimum, a triable issue on whether the nonrenewal and eviction were retaliatory.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Add an explicit causation standard and say the evidence need only create a genuine issue of material fact. Rely on circumstantial evidence, not direct proof, and avoid presenting timing alone as conclusive.

challenges.judge_assessment: The preemption argument is substantial but not airtight on this record. The cited federal authorities support invalidating state law only when the state rule actually requires or permits a discriminatory housing practice. The brief is really attacking application of a neutral Ohio holdover-possession rule and an Eighth District precedent, not pointing to a state enactment that commands discrimination. That makes the conflict argument plausible but not yet dispositive. The court can still accept the brief’s theory if it views the state holdover bar as eliminating a federally protected defense, but the attack has real force.
challenges.suggested_response: The Supremacy Clause does not require this Court to invalidate every Ohio possession rule. It requires only that state law yield to the extent it conflicts with federal law. Under 42 U.S.C. § 3615, any state rule that would permit a discriminatory housing practice is invalid to that extent, and § 3617 prohibits coercion, intimidation, and interference with protected fair-housing activity. To the extent Indian Hills and the holdover rule are applied to foreclose Ms. Masten from asserting a federal retaliation defense to a nonrenewal allegedly motivated by protected activity, they conflict with the Fair Housing Act and must give way.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Narrow the preemption point. Do not say Ohio law is broadly preempted; say only that Ohio law may not be applied here to the extent it bars a federally protected fair-housing retaliation defense or permits retaliatory nonrenewal.

challenges.opponent_argument: Section 3617 does not give a tenant an automatic defense to a possession action simply because she engaged in protected activity. The Ohio landlord-tenant authorities the brief itself relies on recognize a holdover exception: once the lease term has expired and the tenant remains in possession, R.C. 5321.03 permits the landlord to pursue possession notwithstanding retaliation allegations. Indian Hills and the holdover rule therefore cut against, rather than support, treating the nonrenewal/eviction itself as unlawful per se.
challenges.why_it_matters: If the holdover exception applies, Count One can stand even if a separate retaliation claim exists.

challenges.judge_assessment: This attack is directionally supported by the Ohio landlord-tenant materials: they recognize a holdover exception and permit possession actions once the tenancy has ended. But it only gets the landlord so far here. The brief is not asking for a free-standing retaliation defense under state landlord-tenant law alone; it is grounding the claim in the federal Fair Housing Act and arguing that federal law overrides the holdover limitation. So the attack is not wrong as to the state-law backdrop, but it does not by itself defeat the federal-retaliation theory the brief is pressing.
challenges.suggested_response: Section 3617 does not turn every expired lease into a defense to possession, but it does bar a landlord from using nonrenewal and eviction as retaliation for protected fair-housing activity. Indian Hills addressed the Ohio landlord-tenant retaliation statute in a holdover-possession setting; it does not answer whether a landlord may invoke holdover status to insulate a nonrenewal that was motivated by protected conduct. Here, the question is whether K&D’s nonrenewal and eviction were taken because Ms. Masten assisted another tenant and filed her own fair-housing charge. On that issue, the Fair Housing Act supplies an independent defense, and holdover status does not authorize retaliation forbidden by federal law.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Do not argue that the FHA creates an automatic possession defense or that holdover status is irrelevant. Recast the point as a federal anti-retaliation defense to a nonrenewal motivated by protected activity, and make clear that the issue is the landlord’s motive, not the mere expiration of the lease.

challenges.opponent_argument: The Chapter 4112 distinction does not defeat Indian Hills. The brief itself acknowledges that Ohio courts use analogous federal fair-housing law for guidance, and the retrieved Ohio materials show that fair-housing and retaliation defenses in eviction still operate within the landlord-tenant statutory framework. The absence of identical wording in Chapter 4112 does not erase the separate, established holdover rule governing possession actions.
challenges.why_it_matters: If Chapter 4112 is still read alongside the existing holdover-possession rules, Indian Hills remains applicable.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is a fair counter to the Chapter 4112 distinction, but it is not decisive on this record. The brief is right that Chapter 4112 does not mirror the landlord-tenant holdover language, yet Ohio courts often look to federal fair-housing precedent when construing Chapter 4112. That cuts both ways: it helps the brief argue for FHA-consistent treatment, but it also allows Indian Hills reasoning to carry over if the court thinks the possession/holdover rule is conceptually separate from the statutory wording. So the attack has some traction, but the brief has already anticipated most of it.
challenges.suggested_response: Indian Hills should not be imported wholesale into Chapter 4112. Ohio courts have looked to federal fair-housing precedent for guidance in construing Ohio fair-housing law, and the Fair Housing Act recognizes retaliation and discrimination claims arising from adverse housing action. Chapter 4112 does not contain the specific holdover-possession language on which Indian Hills relied in the landlord-tenant context. At minimum, that statutory difference means Indian Hills does not control the question whether a tenant may assert a fair-housing retaliation defense to a nonrenewal alleged to have been motivated by protected activity.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Keep the Chapter 4112 point, but make it modest: the absence of identical holdover language means Indian Hills is not controlling, especially where Ohio courts look to federal fair-housing precedent. Avoid implying that the statutory difference alone resolves the issue.

challenges.why_it_matters: If the court treats policy objections as insufficient to override the holdover rule, the request to overrule Indian Hills fails.

challenges.judge_assessment: The policy attack is the least legal and most rhetorical, but it still matters because the brief is asking the court to abandon Indian Hills. Ohio appellate courts can revisit precedent, but not simply because a party says the rule is harsh. The brief’s policy critique identifies practical unfairness, yet the cited Ohio landlord-tenant authorities still draw a line at holdover status. So the attack is not a knockout, but it undercuts the plea to overrule precedent on policy alone.
challenges.suggested_response: Appellant does not ask this Court to rewrite the statute for policy reasons alone. She asks the Court to construe the statute and Indian Hills consistently with the anti-retaliation purposes of fair-housing law and the public policy of this state. A rule that insulates retaliatory nonrenewals from review chills tenants from exercising protected rights and undermines the enforcement of fair-housing protections. For that reason, even if Indian Hills remains viable in ordinary holdover cases, it should not be extended to shield a retaliatory nonrenewal from judicial review.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Use policy only as supporting context, not as the main ground for reversal. Anchor the request to the remedial purpose of fair-housing law and the conflict with retaliation, rather than a plea to rewrite precedent because it is harsh.

challenges.judge_assessment: This attack would land as a challenge to the analogy, not as a full answer to the brief. L’Orange and Kinney are general public-policy cases, and they do not squarely address a landlord’s decision not to renew a residential lease. The brief’s effort to recast housing retaliation as witness intimidation is imaginative, but the fit is imperfect. Still, the brief’s policy section is supplementary to its FHA and preemption arguments, so defeating the analogy weakens but does not eliminate the overall appeal.
challenges.suggested_response: L’Orange and Kinney are not cited as landlord-tenant cases on all fours with this one. They are cited for the broader Ohio public-policy principle that a party should not be permitted to use a legal power as punishment for protected conduct or for assisting another in vindicating rights. That principle is relevant here because the nonrenewal followed Ms. Masten’s assistance to another tenant and her own fair-housing charge. The authorities are therefore persuasive support for the same conclusion the Fair Housing Act compels: retaliatory use of eviction power should not be sanctioned.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Treat L’Orange, Kinney, and similar authorities as analogies for the public-policy principle against punishment for protected activity, not as direct landlord-tenant holdings. Make the analogy expressly limited and subordinate to the FHA argument.

attacks_proposed.argument: Section 3617 does not give a tenant an automatic defense to a possession action simply because she engaged in protected activity. The Ohio landlord-tenant authorities the brief itself relies on recognize a holdover exception: once the lease term has expired and the tenant remains in possession, R.C. 5321.03 permits the landlord to pursue possession notwithstanding retaliation allegations. Indian Hills and the holdover rule therefore cut against, rather than support, treating the nonrenewal/eviction itself as unlawful per se.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If the holdover exception applies, Count One can stand even if a separate retaliation claim exists.

attacks_proposed.argument: The brief still has to prove causation, not just sequence. The materials cited for retaliation say the issue is proof of the landlord’s motive and that retaliation is typically established only by evidence, not by assumption from timing alone. Here, the brief points to no evidence that conclusively defeats the landlord’s asserted possession rationale or establishes that the nonrenewal was caused by protected activity rather than the lease’s expiration and holdover status.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Without a legally sufficient causal connection, the retaliation theory cannot undo summary judgment on the eviction claim.

attacks_proposed.argument: The Supremacy Clause argument overstates preemption. Section 3615 invalidates state law only to the extent it actually requires or permits a discriminatory housing practice. The brief identifies no Ohio provision that commands discrimination; it objects only to the application of a neutral possession rule in a holdover case. That is not the kind of direct conflict the cited preemption authorities require.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If there is no true conflict, the Ohio court may apply the state holdover-possession rule without violating federal law.

attacks_proposed.argument: The Chapter 4112 distinction does not defeat Indian Hills. The brief itself acknowledges that Ohio courts use analogous federal fair-housing law for guidance, and the retrieved Ohio materials show that fair-housing and retaliation defenses in eviction still operate within the landlord-tenant statutory framework. The absence of identical wording in Chapter 4112 does not erase the separate, established holdover rule governing possession actions.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If Chapter 4112 is still read alongside the existing holdover-possession rules, Indian Hills remains applicable.

attacks_proposed.argument: The policy attack asks the court to rewrite a statute and precedent because the result is said to be harsh. But the Ohio sources addressing retaliation expressly recognize the holdover exception and the landlord’s right to proceed for possession once the tenancy ends. Policy disagreement cannot create a defense the statute does not provide, especially where the governing Ohio materials already draw the line at holdover status.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If the court treats policy objections as insufficient to override the holdover rule, the request to overrule Indian Hills fails.

attacks_proposed.argument: The witness-intimidation analogy is inapt. L’Orange and Kinney concern general public-policy principles and a very different setting; they do not address a landlord’s decision not to renew a residential lease after expiration. The brief’s own landlord-tenant authorities specifically govern retaliation and holdover possession, so those targeted rules—not generalized public-policy analogies—control this case.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If the analogy is rejected, the brief loses its attempt to convert a possession dispute into a freestanding public-policy exception.

judge_assessments.assessment: This is the strongest attack on the brief’s merits. The record does show circumstantial evidence of retaliation—assistance to Thompson, Masten’s own charge, K&D’s knowledge, then nonrenewal and eviction—but the brief still relies heavily on timing and the OCRC probable-cause finding rather than direct proof that the nonrenewal was because of protected activity. Ohio retaliation authorities cited in the source materials treat proof and causation as factual questions, not presumptions. So the attack does not defeat the theory outright, but it meaningfully presses the brief’s weakest link on summary judgment.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief says K&D learned of Masten’s assistance and her own OCRC charge, then issued the 81-day nonrenewal and eviction; it also points to the OCRC probable-cause finding and says the actions occurred after the “exercise of protected activity.”
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Further record support on motive—comparators, landlord statements, inconsistent reasons, or documentary proof tying the notice to the protected activity—would settle this.

judge_assessments.assessment: The preemption argument is substantial but not airtight on this record. The cited federal authorities support invalidating state law only when the state rule actually requires or permits a discriminatory housing practice. The brief is really attacking application of a neutral Ohio holdover-possession rule and an Eighth District precedent, not pointing to a state enactment that commands discrimination. That makes the conflict argument plausible but not yet dispositive. The court can still accept the brief’s theory if it views the state holdover bar as eliminating a federally protected defense, but the attack has real force.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief invokes 42 U.S.C. § 3615, the Supremacy Clause, and cases like Michigan Canners, Swift, Wisconsin, and Larkin to say Ohio courts must yield to the FHA when Ohio law would permit discriminatory or retaliatory eviction.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The key missing piece is a precise identification of the Ohio rule being displaced and why it irreconcilably conflicts with § 3617, rather than merely limiting the forum or timing of the defense.

judge_assessments.assessment: This attack is directionally supported by the Ohio landlord-tenant materials: they recognize a holdover exception and permit possession actions once the tenancy has ended. But it only gets the landlord so far here. The brief is not asking for a free-standing retaliation defense under state landlord-tenant law alone; it is grounding the claim in the federal Fair Housing Act and arguing that federal law overrides the holdover limitation. So the attack is not wrong as to the state-law backdrop, but it does not by itself defeat the federal-retaliation theory the brief is pressing.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief says § 3617 forbids coercion/interference, that nonrenewal can be retaliatory, and that Indian Hills should not control FHA claims because the federal statute lacks the landlord-tenant holdover language found in R.C. 5321.03(A)(4).
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Whether the appellate court treats the holdover rule as merely a state-law limit on retaliation defenses or as compatible with the FHA is the controlling legal question.

judge_assessments.assessment: This is a fair counter to the Chapter 4112 distinction, but it is not decisive on this record. The brief is right that Chapter 4112 does not mirror the landlord-tenant holdover language, yet Ohio courts often look to federal fair-housing precedent when construing Chapter 4112. That cuts both ways: it helps the brief argue for FHA-consistent treatment, but it also allows Indian Hills reasoning to carry over if the court thinks the possession/holdover rule is conceptually separate from the statutory wording. So the attack has some traction, but the brief has already anticipated most of it.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief says Chapter 4112 lacks the holdover language found in R.C. 5321.03(A)(4), cites Wooten and Matthews for looking to federal precedent, and argues that the absence of identical wording means Indian Hills should not be imported wholesale into Ohio fair-housing law.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: A court would likely focus on whether Chapter 4112 independently supplies a retaliation defense in a holdover posture, or whether the landlord-tenant holdover rule still governs possession separately.

judge_assessments.assessment: The policy attack is the least legal and most rhetorical, but it still matters because the brief is asking the court to abandon Indian Hills. Ohio appellate courts can revisit precedent, but not simply because a party says the rule is harsh. The brief’s policy critique identifies practical unfairness, yet the cited Ohio landlord-tenant authorities still draw a line at holdover status. So the attack is not a knockout, but it undercuts the plea to overrule precedent on policy alone.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief says Indian Hills is overinclusive, creates a safe harbor for landlords, chills tenants from exercising rights, and should be reversed as against public policy.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: A stronger overruling argument would need doctrinal inconsistency, not just policy objections—such as conflict with later Ohio authority or statutory amendment.

judge_assessments.assessment: This attack would land as a challenge to the analogy, not as a full answer to the brief. L’Orange and Kinney are general public-policy cases, and they do not squarely address a landlord’s decision not to renew a residential lease. The brief’s effort to recast housing retaliation as witness intimidation is imaginative, but the fit is imperfect. Still, the brief’s policy section is supplementary to its FHA and preemption arguments, so defeating the analogy weakens but does not eliminate the overall appeal.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief directly uses L’Orange, Kinney, and Porter to argue that punishing Masten for helping another tenant is contrary to public policy and akin to witness intimidation.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The key question is whether Ohio would recognize a housing-retaliation public-policy exception independent of the FHA/statutory arguments; the cited cases do not clearly establish that.

results.verdict: partly persuasive but exposed on causation and the holdover
results.assessment: The brief has real force in its federal-preemption and anti-retaliation framing, and it plausibly argues that Indian Hills should not be imported wholesale into the Chapter 4112 or FHA setting. But as written it is still vulnerable on the central merits: it leans too heavily on timing and does not clearly defeat the landlord’s asserted possession rationale or show that the nonrenewal was caused by protected activity. The holdover authorities also cut against treating the expired lease as irrelevant, so the brief needs a tighter explanation of why federal law overrides that backdrop. The policy analogies are the weakest part and should not carry the argument.

challenges.judge_assessment: This lands. The cited landlord-tenant sources do not support the brief’s blanket statement that Civ.R. 13(A) is simply inapplicable to all FED-related proceedings. Source 2 says the rule does not apply when the eviction complaint seeks only possession, but source 4 shows a Chapter 1923 case may also include rent and other damages. The brief does respond by arguing the later personal-injury claim is not logically related to the prior actions, but it does not really answer the separate problem that appellees relied on a 2004 back-rent/breach-of-lease action as well as the FED case.
challenges.suggested_response: Appellees’ res judicata argument fails because they have not shown that appellant’s personal-injury claim was a compulsory counterclaim in the proceedings they identify. As the landlord-tenant authorities recognize, Civ.R. 13(A) does not apply where an eviction complaint alleges only possession, and appellees’ reliance on Chapter 1923 does not establish that appellant was required to assert a tort claim in a separate back-rent or breach-of-lease action. At minimum, appellees have not shown that this personal-injury claim arises out of the same transaction or occurrence as the prior possession or rent proceedings, so res judicata does not bar this action.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Narrow the res judicata section so it does not claim Civ.R. 13(A) is categorically inapplicable to every Chapter 1923 proceeding. The brief should instead concede that the rule may not apply to a possession-only eviction, then argue that appellees have not shown appellant’s separate personal-injury claim was a compulsory counterclaim in either the FED action or any later back-rent action.

Nothing in the brief shows the table was hidden, latent, or otherwise non-obvious. The fact that the table ultimately struck him does not eliminate the doctrine.
challenges.why_it_matters: If the table's condition was open and obvious, appellees owed no duty on this theory and summary judgment should be affirmed.
