challenges.judge_assessment: This is a strong attack. Source 40 states the open-and-obvious doctrine turns on whether the danger was open and obvious, not on whether the plaintiff voluntarily chose to encounter it. The brief answers only by saying the table struck appellant and he did not choose the danger, which does not really meet the doctrinal point. The problem for appellant is that the record describes a six-foot folding table leaning in the storage room; if that condition was obvious, appellees owed no duty under this theory regardless of how the impact occurred.
challenges.suggested_response: Appellees were not entitled to summary judgment under the open-and-obvious doctrine because they did not establish, as a matter of law, that the condition in the storage room was so open and obvious that appellant had no duty-based claim. The record shows only that appellant was directed into a storage room to retrieve his belongings and that a six-foot folding table leaning against a wall either fell or was knocked onto him. Those facts do not establish that appellees were relieved of their duty of reasonable care as a matter of law.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Rewrite the open-and-obvious discussion to focus on whether appellees proved the condition was open and obvious as a matter of law, not on whether appellant voluntarily chose to encounter it. Do not argue that a six-foot table can never be a dangerous condition; that overstates the record.

challenges.why_it_matters: If the circumstantial facts do not show the accident would not ordinarily occur without negligence, res ipsa does not create a triable issue.

challenges.judge_assessment: This has some force, but it is not devastating. Source 53 supports the Civ.R. 56(E) burden point, and the brief does rely on inference language rather than a fully explained mechanism of how the table fell or was knocked. That said, the brief does point to specific facts: exclusive control of the room, the scheduled cleanout, the table’s placement, and testimony that the table should not have been there. The real issue is whether those facts are enough to satisfy res ipsa’s second prong, not whether appellant offered nothing at all.
challenges.suggested_response: Res ipsa loquitur permits, but does not require, an inference of negligence from these circumstances. Appellees controlled the storage room, appellant was brought there by appointment to retrieve his belongings, and the evidence shows the table was in appellees’ control and should not have been there. Taken together and construed most strongly in appellant’s favor, those facts permit a jury to infer that the injury would not have occurred absent negligence.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Soften the res ipsa point from certainty to permissible inference. The brief should say the circumstantial evidence allows a jury to infer negligence, not that the second element is conclusively proved.

The brief does identify Ball as community manager, says employees were present, and ties the cleanout meeting to appellees’ business. That gives some scope-of-employment support. What is missing is a precise identification of which employee moved or knocked the table and how that act fit within job duties. So the attack exposes a gap, but it does not clearly defeat vicarious liability on its own.
challenges.suggested_response: The record supports a factual issue whether the employees present in the storage room were acting within the course and scope of their employment. Ms. Ball testified that she arranged the cleanout, set the date and time, and had employees present in the building’s storage room to clear out the room and identify appellant’s belongings. From that evidence, a jury could find that the acts surrounding the table incident occurred while appellees’ employees were performing assigned work for the apartment complex.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Keep respondeat superior, but narrow it to the record-supported point that the cleanout was arranged by the community manager and carried out by employees acting for the apartment complex. Do not imply the record proves exactly which employee moved the table.

challenges.why_it_matters: If appellant did not produce specific facts on breach, causation, and scope, summary judgment was properly entered.

The summary-judgment record includes deposition testimony and appellees’ admissions that the storage room was under their exclusive control, that appellant was directed there at a set time to retrieve his belongings, and that the table involved in the incident was under appellees’ control. Source 40 says the relevant question is whether the danger was open and obvious; if it was, the landowner owes no duty. The brief's own facts describe a six-foot folding table leaning against a wall in a room appellant entered to sort belongings. Nothing in the brief shows the table was hidden, latent, or otherwise non-obvious. The fact that the table ultimately struck him does not eliminate the doctrine.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If the table's condition was open and obvious, appellees owed no duty on this theory and summary judgment should be affirmed.

attacks_proposed.argument: Res ipsa loquitur fails because the brief only shows exclusive control of the room, not exclusive control of the actual instrumentality at the moment of injury. The doctrine requires control of the thing that caused the harm. Here, the brief says only that the storage room was under appellees' control and that the table was still being used elsewhere in the building. That leaves a gap: the brief never ties the specific table movement or placement to exclusive appellee control at the time it struck appellant.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Without exclusive control of the instrumentality, the inference of negligence does not arise and res ipsa cannot carry the negligence claim to a jury.

attacks_proposed.argument: Even if control were assumed, the brief still lacks the second res ipsa element. Saying that "either ordinary care was not used, or one of the appellees caused the table to fall" is speculation, not proof that the accident would not ordinarily occur absent negligence. Under Civ.R. 56(E), appellant had to point to specific facts showing a trial issue; he cannot replace that burden with a bare inference stacked on top of an unexplained accident.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If the circumstantial facts do not show the accident would not ordinarily occur without negligence, res ipsa does not create a triable issue.

attacks_proposed.argument: The respondeat superior theory is missing the critical scope-of-employment showing. The brief says Ball arranged the cleanout and that employees were present, but it never identifies which employee allegedly caused the table incident or explains how moving, leaving, or knocking the table was within the scope of that employee's job duties. Presence in the storage room is not the same as proof that the tortious act was performed in the course and scope of employment.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Without scope-of-employment evidence, the corporate appellees cannot be held liable vicariously for the table incident.

attacks_proposed.argument: The brief invokes summary judgment standards but does not meet them. Civ.R. 56(E) requires the nonmoving party to set forth specific facts showing a genuine issue for trial. Here, the brief repeatedly relies on broad conclusions such as "at the very least" genuine issues remain, or that a jury "can infer" negligence, while leaving the actual causal mechanism of the table incident unexplained. That is not a Civ.R. 56 response to a supported motion; it is an invitation for speculation.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If appellant did not produce specific facts on breach, causation, and scope, summary judgment was properly entered.

judge_assessments.assessment: This lands. The cited landlord-tenant sources do not support the brief’s blanket statement that Civ.R. 13(A) is simply inapplicable to all FED-related proceedings. Source 2 says the rule does not apply when the eviction complaint seeks only possession, but source 4 shows a Chapter 1923 case may also include rent and other damages. The brief does respond by arguing the later personal-injury claim is not logically related to the prior actions, but it does not really answer the separate problem that appellees relied on a 2004 back-rent/breach-of-lease action as well as the FED case.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: It says the 2003 FED and 2004 back-rent/breach-of-lease cases do not make this claim a compulsory counterclaim because the injury claim is not logically related and the common-area/Sherman facts are different.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Need the actual pleadings and judgment entries from the 2004 back-rent case to see whether it was part of the prior litigation and whether the claim would have been compulsory there.

judge_assessments.assessment: This is a strong attack. Source 40 states the open-and-obvious doctrine turns on whether the danger was open and obvious, not on whether the plaintiff voluntarily chose to encounter it. The brief answers only by saying the table struck appellant and he did not choose the danger, which does not really meet the doctrinal point. The problem for appellant is that the record describes a six-foot folding table leaning in the storage room; if that condition was obvious, appellees owed no duty under this theory regardless of how the impact occurred.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: It says appellant did not encounter the table as a known danger; the table struck him, and a six-foot folding table is not an open-and-obvious dangerous condition as a matter of law.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Need record evidence about visibility, lighting, placement, and whether appellant knew the table was there before the impact.

judge_assessments.assessment: This has some force, but it is not devastating. Source 53 supports the Civ.R. 56(E) burden point, and the brief does rely on inference language rather than a fully explained mechanism of how the table fell or was knocked. That said, the brief does point to specific facts: exclusive control of the room, the scheduled cleanout, the table’s placement, and testimony that the table should not have been there. The real issue is whether those facts are enough to satisfy res ipsa’s second prong, not whether appellant offered nothing at all.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: It says appellees’ exclusive control plus the circumstances allow a jury to infer negligence under res ipsa loquitur.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Need the actual res ipsa authorities and any record evidence about how the table was stored or moved, because that determines whether the inference is permissible or just speculation.

judge_assessments.assessment: This is a fair appellate point but not a clean loser on this record. The brief does identify Ball as community manager, says employees were present, and ties the cleanout meeting to appellees’ business. That gives some scope-of-employment support. What is missing is a precise identification of which employee moved or knocked the table and how that act fit within job duties. So the attack exposes a gap, but it does not clearly defeat vicarious liability on its own.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: It says Ball arranged the cleanout, employees were present, and the tort was caused either directly by Ball or another Lakeshore Towers employee acting within the scope of employment.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Need evidence tying the specific table incident to an employee’s job duties, not just presence in the room.

judge_assessments.assessment: This lands only partially. Source 53 correctly states the Civ.R. 56 burden, and the brief does lean heavily on broad conclusions in places. But unlike a bare-response case, the brief also quotes deposition excerpts and specific facts about the room, the table, and the encounter. So the attack does not show a total failure to respond under Civ.R. 56(E); it instead frames the real dispute over whether those facts create a genuine issue.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: It quotes depositions and says the facts show material disputes on negligence, res ipsa, open and obvious, and respondeat superior.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Need to compare the cited deposition excerpts with the actual summary-judgment record to see whether the facts were admissible and whether they were enough to create a triable issue.

judge_assessments.assessment: This overreaches. The cited sources do not establish that every cleanout-related injury is part of the same transaction or occurrence as a landlord-tenant possession/back-rent dispute, and the brief already argues the opposite by distinguishing the injury claim from the prior cases. On this record, the court is unlikely to treat the storage-room accident as automatically part of the same basic controversy without more about the earlier pleadings.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: It says the personal-injury claim is not logically related to the prior FED or back-rent proceedings and involved different issues and a different setting.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Need the actual prior complaints to see whether the cleanout/storage-room dispute was pleaded or litigated there.

judge_assessments.assessment: This does not land on the cited authority. Source 53 is a summary-judgment case, not a res ipsa source, so it does not supply the control rule the attack invokes. The brief also has some record support for appellees’ exclusive control over the storage room and the table’s presence in appellees’ operations, so this is not a clean authority-based knockout.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: It says the storage room was under appellees’ exclusive control and the table was still being used by appellees elsewhere in the building.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Need the actual res ipsa authorities cited in the brief and the precise record on who controlled the table, not just the room.

results.verdict: mixed and vulnerable on the central liability theories
results.assessment: The brief reads as workable on the facts, but it is not yet persuasive where appellees’ strongest defenses are involved. Its biggest weakness is the overbroad res judicata argument: it treats Civ.R. 13(A) as categorically irrelevant to all FED-related proceedings, which the cited landlord-tenant authorities do not support. The open-and-obvious discussion is also underdeveloped because it answers the doctrine with voluntariness instead of the condition’s obviousness. Res ipsa and respondeat superior have some factual support, but both still leave key gaps in the causal mechanism and scope-of-employment showing. The summary-judgment presentation has facts, but it leans too hard on inference language.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is the strongest attack. Hake requires both exclusive control and circumstances showing the accident would not have happened absent lack of ordinary care. The brief proves control over the room and argues the table was under appellees' control, but the record also says the table 'fell or was knocked' while several people were present. That leaves an alternative-cause problem the brief does not eliminate. On this record, a court could well say res ipsa is too speculative to defeat summary judgment.
challenges.suggested_response: At minimum, the evidence permits a jury to infer negligence under res ipsa loquitur. Appellees controlled the locked storage room, arranged appellant’s presence there, and the table that struck appellant was within their control. Although appellant could not identify every act that led to the table’s fall, the circumstances are such that a jury could conclude the accident would not have occurred had ordinary care been used. The question whether appellees were negligent is therefore for the trier of fact, not for summary judgment.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Make res ipsa loquitur a permissive-inference argument, not a certainty argument. Tie the inference to appellees’ control of the room and the table, but do not claim the record eliminates every other possible cause.

challenges.opponent_argument: The brief overstates the law when it says Civ.R. 13(A) does not apply to forcible-entry-and-detainer cases. Civ.R. 1(C) applies the Civil Rules in special statutory proceedings unless a rule is clearly inapplicable, and R.C. 1923.081 expressly contemplates residential FED trials that also resolve rent and other damages. Source 2 likewise limits the nonapplication point to eviction complaints that seek only possession. The brief never distinguishes a pure possession-only FED from the back-rent proceeding appellees relied on, so its categorical exclusion theory is too broad.
challenges.why_it_matters: If Civ.R. 13(A) is not categorically unavailable, appellant loses the core premise of his res judicata rebuttal.

challenges.suggested_response: Even if the Court does not resolve appellant’s status as an invitee as a matter of law, appellees’ own evidence shows that appellant was expressly directed to come to a locked storage room under appellees’ control to retrieve his belongings. On those facts, appellees owed appellant at least a duty to exercise ordinary care in the manner they conducted the cleanup and in maintaining the room in a reasonably safe condition. Summary judgment was therefore improper.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Avoid calling appellant an invitee as a settled matter of law. Recast the point as a duty owed to a lawful entrant whom appellees expressly invited into a locked room they controlled.

challenges.judge_assessment: Ohio's open-and-obvious doctrine is a genuine defense issue, and the brief's statement that nobody can call a six-foot folding table a dangerous condition is too categorical. The better question is whether the condition was open and obvious on these facts, not whether folding tables can never be dangerous. The brief answers by emphasizing that the table struck appellant rather than being a hazard he knowingly encountered, but that does not fully take the defense off the table.
challenges.suggested_response: Appellees have not shown that the open-and-obvious doctrine bars this claim as a matter of law. Appellant was directed into a locked room under appellees’ control to retrieve his belongings, and the table that struck him did not present a hazard that he knowingly chose to encounter. On this record, whether the condition was open and obvious is at least a factual question for the jury.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Stop arguing that a folding table can never be a dangerous condition. Argue instead that appellees have not shown, as a matter of law, that the condition was open and obvious to appellant before the accident.

attacks_proposed.argument: The brief overstates the law when it says Civ.R. 13(A) does not apply to forcible-entry-and-detainer cases. Civ.R. 1(C) applies the Civil Rules in special statutory proceedings unless a rule is clearly inapplicable, and R.C. 1923.081 expressly contemplates residential FED trials that also resolve rent and other damages. Source 2 likewise limits the nonapplication point to eviction complaints that seek only possession. The brief never distinguishes a pure possession-only FED from the back-rent proceeding appellees relied on, so its categorical exclusion theory is too broad.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If Civ.R. 13(A) is not categorically unavailable, appellant loses the core premise of his res judicata rebuttal.

attacks_proposed.argument: The brief treats the prior eviction and back-rent litigation as if the only question were whether Kerr was named in every earlier case. That is not the Ohio test. The analysis turns on whether the present claim should have been asserted in the earlier transaction, and the brief itself concedes a later back-rent/breach action. Sources 6, 8, 23, and 24 show Ohio landlord-tenant litigation is structured to resolve related monetary and tenancy claims together; the brief does not explain why this injury claim was outside that controversy.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If the prior rent litigation is part of the same controversy, the res judicata defense remains viable notwithstanding the brief's party-based distinction.

attacks_proposed.argument: The 'not the same transaction or occurrence' argument is too thin because it relies almost entirely on the labels 'storage-room injury' and 'rent/eviction.' Rettig's logical-relation approach asks whether the claims arise from the same controversy and whether separate trials would duplicate effort. Here, the brief's own facts tie the injury to the landlord-controlled storage-room cleanup that was part of the tenancy dispute, and the statutory materials show Ohio permits rent and related damages to be tried in the same residential FED framework. That is not a complete showing that the tort claim was outside the earlier transaction.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If the injury claim is transactionally related to the earlier landlord-tenant dispute, it should have been raised then and the summary-judgment ruling stands.

attacks_proposed.argument: The brief does not establish invitee status as a matter of law. Its authorities describe a landowner's duties to invitees generally, but the facts it supplies show only that Kerr was a tenant allowed into a locked storage room to retrieve his own belongings. That is not the classic business-invitee scenario, and the brief cites no authority turning a tenant's retrieval visit into invitee status merely because management scheduled it.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Without invitee status, the claimed duty of ordinary care is not clearly established and the negligence theory weakens substantially.

attacks_proposed.argument: Res ipsa loquitur does not carry the brief over the summary-judgment hurdle because the brief never eliminates other plausible causes. Hake requires more than showing the room was controlled by appellees; it requires circumstances showing the injury would not have occurred absent a lack of ordinary care. The brief's own account is that the table 'fell or was knocked' while multiple people were in the room. That uncertainty cuts against the inference the brief wants a jury to draw, and source 56 underscores that causation still must be shown, not assumed.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If res ipsa is unavailable, appellant is left with a speculative causation theory rather than evidence sufficient to avoid summary judgment.

attacks_proposed.argument: The brief's open-and-obvious argument is too categorical. Ohio law asks whether the condition was open and obvious; if it was, the landowner owes no duty. The brief cannot avoid that doctrine simply by saying a six-foot folding table is never a 'dangerous condition' as a matter of law. Its own facts show only that the table was in the room and struck Kerr; they do not show why the condition was hidden or why the defense could not apply.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If the open-and-obvious doctrine remains in play, appellees retain a complete duty defense against the premises-liability theory.

judge_assessments.assessment: This is the strongest attack. Hake requires both exclusive control and circumstances showing the accident would not have happened absent lack of ordinary care. The brief proves control over the room and argues the table was under appellees' control, but the record also says the table 'fell or was knocked' while several people were present. That leaves an alternative-cause problem the brief does not eliminate. On this record, a court could well say res ipsa is too speculative to defeat summary judgment.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief says appellees had exclusive control of the storage room; appellant did not cause the injury; and because the table struck him, a jury can infer negligence under res ipsa loquitur.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Whether Ohio applies res ipsa when the instrumentality may have been moved by multiple people in the room, and whether exclusive control of the room is enough when the exact cause of the table's movement is uncertain.

The brief's Haney point helps for a pure possession FED, but it does not fully answer appellees' back-rent-action theory. results.verdict: Partially persuasive, but exposed on its broadest legal clai
results.assessment: The brief has some real force on the facts: it shows appellees controlled the locked room, directed appellant there, and presents enough to argue ordinary care and a jury question on open-and-obvious. But it is most vulnerable where it overstates the law. The categorical Civ.R. 13(A) / res judicata position is too broad, especially given the back-rent-action theory and the lack of a clear distinction between a possession-only FED and a broader proceeding. It is also weak on res ipsa because it does not eliminate alternative causes, and invitee status is not firmly established. The research did not settle those factual status questions.

challenges.judge_assessment: This lands. The cited Ohio materials do not make a written lease or cash rent the exclusive way to create tenant status. Source 4 expressly recognizes an employee who may lease and reside pursuant to a contract of employment, and source 38 says a rental agreement can be oral. The brief mostly answers with 'no written contract' and 'no rent,' but it does not grapple with the employee-tenant/implicit-agreement theory. On this record, appellees risk losing the core premise that appellant was categorically a non-tenant.
challenges.suggested_response: Appellant relies on authorities recognizing that an employee may, in some circumstances, occupy residential premises pursuant to a contract of employment and that a rental agreement may be oral. Those authorities do not establish tenant status here, however, because they still require evidence of an agreement creating a possessory right in the premises. Appellant identifies no such evidence in this record, and the cases she cites do not transform an employment-related occupancy into a tenancy as a matter of law.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Revise the tenancy discussion to acknowledge that Ohio law can recognize an employee tenant or an oral rental agreement, and do not present the absence of a written lease and cash rent as automatically defeating tenancy. The response should focus on the lack of record evidence showing any oral, implied, or employment-based agreement that gave appellant a right of occupancy as a tenant.

The phrase "may be had" is a grant of authority to bring FED proceedings; it is not an affirmative authorization for self-help removal. results.assessment: The brief’s strongest feature is that it repeatedly presses the absence of a written lease and cash rent, but that is also its main weakness: the supplied Ohio materials do not make those facts dispositive, and they leave open an employee-tenant or oral/implied-agreement theory that the brief does not really confront. Its other serious problem is the leap from R.C. 1923.02(A)’s permissive FED language to a claimed right of self-help removal; the cited authority supports permissive filing, not bypassing court process. The broader “these cases are only fact-specific” attack is less damaging. The research did not leave a settled factual record showing no occupancy agreement.

The managed-source materials define a rental agreement as any agreement, written or oral, concerning use and occupancy, and they recognize that an employee may be an "employee tenant" under a contract of employment. On the record here, Appellant was given a room as an accommodation for her employment, so the absence of a separate rent check does not, by itself, eliminate the possibility of a rental or tenancy arrangement.
challenges.why_it_matters: If an employment-based occupancy can qualify as a rental agreement or employee tenancy, the brief's premise that FED was optional collapses.

record_sources.quote: "There was no written contract of employment." ... "Appellant admits that she did not pay rent to the Wallaces and that nothing was taken from her employment check for rent" ... "Appellant was provided with a room to stay in while on duty as an accommodation for her employment."

challenges.judge_assessment: This lands hard. The Ohio materials cited by the attack expressly recognize that a rental agreement can be oral and that an employee can be an "employee tenant" under a contract of employment. The brief's "no written lease + no cash rent" formulation does not answer that point. On this record, the court could not treat the absence of a separate rent check as automatically defeating tenancy as a matter of law if the room was part of the employment bargain.
challenges.suggested_response: Whether, on this record, Appellant established any oral or written rental agreement or other employment-based tenancy that would make her a tenant under R.C. 5321.01 and trigger the exclusive procedures of R.C. 5321.15(A). Ohio law recognizes that a rental agreement may be oral, and that an employee may in some circumstances be an employee tenant, but the record here contains no evidence of any rental agreement and shows only that Appellant was provided a room as an accommodation of her employment, paid no rent, and maintained a separate residence. On those facts, the trial court correctly concluded that Appellant was not shown to be a tenant.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Narrow the issue statement so it does not treat the absence of a written lease or a separate rent check as conclusive by itself. Anchor the point in the record: no rental agreement was shown, the room was provided as an employment accommodation, and Appellant maintained a separate residence; then argue that those facts do not establish tenant status on this record.

challenges.opponent_argument: The summary-judgment theory is overbroad because the record the brief relies on does not rule out an employment-based tenancy as a matter of law. The cited sources explain that Ohio recognizes employee-tenancy arrangements and that a rental agreement may be oral or implied from the parties' conduct. Here, the room was provided as an accommodation for Appellant's work, which is evidence a factfinder could treat as consideration or part of the employment bargain, not merely gratuitous lodging.
challenges.why_it_matters: If the employment accommodation could support a tenancy theory, Counts II, V, VI, and VII should not have been disposed of on summary judgment.

record_sources.title: record-01-record
record_sources.quote: "Plaintiff was not a tenant pursuant to Ohio's Landlord Tenant Act and no tenancy was created as a result of her employment... No rental agreement was entered into between the parties. No rent was paid by the plaintiff to the defendants. In fact, plaintiff paid rent to and maintained a residence separate from her place of employment. Therefore, plaintiff's claims based on tenancy, Counts II, V., VI and VII, must fail as a matter of law."

challenges.judge_assessment: This is a serious summary-judgment attack. The brief relies on the same facts, but the cited Ohio materials allow a tenancy to arise from an oral or implied arrangement and recognize employee-tenancy as a real category. If the room was part of the compensation package, a factfinder could treat that as consideration. The record as summarized in the brief does not conclusively negate that possibility.
challenges.suggested_response: The trial court did not err in granting summary judgment because the materials before it showed no genuine issue of material fact on tenancy. The court found that no rental agreement was entered into, no rent was paid, Appellant maintained a separate residence, and the room in the Wallace home was provided as an accommodation for her employment. While Ohio law recognizes that an employee may in some circumstances lease and reside in premises pursuant to a contract of employment, Appellant identified no evidence creating a rental agreement or other tenancy on these facts. Accordingly, Counts II, V, VI, and VII failed as a matter of law.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Tighten the summary-judgment discussion to avoid implying that the court rejected an employee-tenancy theory merely because there was no separate rent payment. Emphasize instead that the record contained no evidence of any rental agreement, and that the undisputed facts showed an accommodation for employment, not a leasehold.

challenges.opponent_argument: The brief's categorical rule that a former live-in employee may be removed without filing FED if there is no separate rental agreement and no rent is not found in the statutes it cites. R.C. 1923.01 and 1923.02 are written in broad terms and cover persons who unlawfully hold possession, including occupiers without color of title; the managed-source material likewise notes that the FED statute does not on its face limit defendants to tenants. On the brief's own authorities, the absence of a conventional landlord-tenant relationship does not create a free-standing self-help exception.
challenges.why_it_matters: If Chapter 1923 already contemplates occupiers and unlawful holders, appellees cannot justify self-help removal by recasting the case as merely a non-tenant employment dispute.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is the brief's weakest legal jump. The cited statutes are broad and include occupiers, but they do not themselves state a free-standing right for an owner or employer to use self-help against a residential occupant. The brief's assertion that a former live-in employee may be removed without filing FED if there is no separate lease or rent is not directly supported by the authorities it cites, and the court could view that as an unsupported expansion of Ohio law.
challenges.suggested_response: R.C. 5321.15(A) makes the FED procedure exclusive only where the parties stand in a residential landlord-tenant relationship. Here, the trial court found that Appellant was not a tenant, that no rental agreement existed, that no rent was paid, and that she maintained a separate residence. On that record, Appellant cannot convert Chapter 1923 into the exclusive remedy for this employment-based occupancy dispute, and her wrongful-eviction theory fails.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Delete the unsupported suggestion that a former employee may affirmatively use self-help to remove an occupant. Keep only the supported proposition that, absent a tenancy, Chapter 1923 and R.C. 5321.15(A) do not make FED the exclusive remedy, and that Appellant did not establish the landlord-tenant relationship those statutes address.

challenges.opponent_argument: The brief overstates Ogle, Stone, and Amick. The record descriptions of those cases are rent-free, no-lease family or cohabitation disputes; they do not address a live-in home-health worker who was furnished a room as part of her job. The managed-source material on employee tenants shows that Ohio treats employment-based occupancy as a distinct category, and Chapter 5321 has modified the common-law rules in that setting. Those cases therefore do not control the employee-occupancy question presented here.
challenges.why_it_matters: If the cited cases are materially different, they cannot be used to establish a blanket rule that a fired live-in worker may be removed without first using FED.

record_sources.quote: "An individual who lives in a residence with another without a rental agreement and without the payment of rent is not a tenant and cannot maintain an action for wrongful eviction." ... "During this entire period, appellant and Michael lived in the house rent-free. It is undisputed that there was no written or oral lease" ... "In the case sub judice, no lease of any kind was established"

challenges.judge_assessment: This attack has real force on the authorities, but it is not fatal by itself. Ogle, Stone, and Amick, as described in the brief, are rent-free cohabitation cases, not live-in employment cases. The brief does not squarely answer the employee-occupancy distinction; it mainly says those cases show that no tenancy exists without a rental agreement and rent. That makes the analogy vulnerable, though the court can still treat them as persuasive on the tenant-definition question.
challenges.suggested_response: Ogle, Stone, and Amick are cited not because they involved live-in employment, but because they correctly state the governing tenancy principle: where the record shows no rental agreement and no rent, the occupant is not a tenant and cannot maintain a wrongful-eviction claim based on landlord-tenant statutes. Although those cases arose in cohabitation settings, their legal rule remains the same here. The undisputed facts still show that Appellant was housed as an incident of employment, not as a tenant under a rental agreement.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Acknowledge that Ogle, Stone, and Amick are not employee-occupancy cases, and use them only for the narrower statutory point they actually support: without a rental agreement and rent, Ohio courts have held that an occupant is not a tenant. Add a sentence distinguishing the employee-accommodation setting from the cohabitation cases.

challenges.opponent_argument: The commercial-premises cases the brief relies on do not create a residential self-help exception. Northfield Park and Craig Wrecking dealt with commercial leasing, not a residential home-occupancy arrangement tied to employment. The broader statutory materials the brief cites show that Chapter 1923 is not limited on its face to tenants and landlords alone, so those commercial cases do not support converting a residential occupant's status into a license for self-help removal.
challenges.why_it_matters: If the commercial cases are not analogous, the brief loses its attempt to use them to justify bypassing FED in a residential setting.

judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief says no written contract of employment was made, Appellant did not pay rent, nothing was withheld for rent, she kept a separate residence, and the room was provided as an accommodation for employment.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Full text of the employee-tenant authorities, especially whether Ohio treats lodging provided as part of compensation as consideration for a rental agreement.

judge_assessments.assessment: This is a serious summary-judgment attack. The brief relies on the same facts, but the cited Ohio materials allow a tenancy to arise from an oral or implied arrangement and recognize employee-tenancy as a real category. If the room was part of the compensation package, a factfinder could treat that as consideration. The record as summarized in the brief does not conclusively negate that possibility.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The trial court found no rental agreement, no rent paid, and a separate residence, and concluded that Plaintiff was not a tenant under Ohio's Landlord Tenant Act; therefore Counts II, V, VI, and VII failed as a matter of law.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Whether Ohio precedent treats employee-provided housing as a question of law on undisputed facts or as a factual issue when the room is furnished as part of the job.

judge_assessments.assessment: This is the brief's weakest legal jump. The cited statutes are broad and include occupiers, but they do not themselves state a free-standing right for an owner or employer to use self-help against a residential occupant. The brief's assertion that a former live-in employee may be removed without filing FED if there is no separate lease or rent is not directly supported by the authorities it cites, and the court could view that as an unsupported expansion of Ohio law.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief says that if there is no tenancy, Appellees were not relegated to the exclusive remedy of an FED action, and it goes further to say that a former employee may take steps to remove the occupant without filing FED, or may elect FED.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Ohio authority on whether non-tenant residential occupants may be removed by self-help, and whether Chapter 1923 is merely permissive or functionally required once possession is disputed.

judge_assessments.assessment: This attack has real force on the authorities, but it is not fatal by itself. Ogle, Stone, and Amick, as described in the brief, are rent-free cohabitation cases, not live-in employment cases. The brief does not squarely answer the employee-occupancy distinction; it mainly says those cases show that no tenancy exists without a rental agreement and rent. That makes the analogy vulnerable, though the court can still treat them as persuasive on the tenant-definition question.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief relies on Ogle, Stone, and Amick to say that where there is no rental agreement and no rent, there is no tenancy and FED is not the only way to remove the occupant.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Full opinions in Ogle, Stone, and Amick, plus any Ohio cases specifically addressing live-in employees or caregivers.

judge_assessments.assessment: This is a fair analogy attack, but it is not the best avenue to defeat the brief. Northfield Park and Craig Wrecking are commercial-premises cases, so they do not directly answer what happens in a residential home-occupancy arrangement tied to employment. Still, the brief cites them only for the narrower proposition that Chapter 1923 is not universally exclusive outside residential-tenant situations. The court can simply view them as inapposite rather than wrong, which limits the damage.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief uses Northfield Park, Craig Wrecking, Ashbury, and Smith to argue that Chapter 1923 is not exclusive in non-residential/commercial situations and that exclusivity is expressly stated only for residential tenants in R.C. 5321.15(A).
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Whether any Ohio decision extends the commercial self-help reasoning into a residential employee-occupancy setting.

results.verdict: Not yet persuasive on the central tenant-status and remedy q
results.assessment: The brief has a workable theme on the undisputed absence of a written lease and separate rent, but it is exposed where it treats that as automatically defeating tenancy and as authorizing removal without FED. The strongest challenges show that Ohio materials recognize oral or implied rental agreements and even employee-tenancy, so the record as summarized does not conclusively rule out a tenancy or employment-based rental arrangement. It also overreaches in using broad statutes and cohabitation or commercial cases to support a residential self-help rule that the cited authorities do not clearly supply. The research did not settle whether the employee-occupancy facts can be distinguished from tenancy as a matter of law.

record_sources.title: record-01-record
record_sources.quote: IT IS THEREFORE ORDERED, ADJUDGED AND DECREED that real properties located at ... 8127 Cedar Road ... be transferred into the Estate of Anthony Notarian immediately. ... On February 1, 2023. See attached Exhibits 10 and 13. Title to property passes upon the proper execution and delivery of a deed ... Delivery of this deed to the probate court constitutes delivery of title, thus the Estate has title to the Premises.

challenges.judge_assessment: This lands. Ohio authority cited by both sides makes present title central to the right of possession, and the record excerpt does not itself show the mechanics of delivery needed to make the deed effective. The brief does say defendants executed a deed on February 1, 2023 and cites Wayne/Gordon for the proposition that delivery passes title, but the contested point is whether this record actually establishes a legally effective delivery to the Estate rather than just an executed instrument. If the court is unconvinced on delivery, summary judgment on possession fails.
challenges.suggested_response: The probate court ordered the Cedar Road property returned to the Estate, and defendants thereafter executed a deed conveying the Premises to the Estate on February 1, 2023. Plaintiff relies on those orders and the executed deed, together with Wayne Bldg. & Loan Co. of Wooster v. Yarborough, for the settled rule that title passes upon proper execution and delivery of a deed, not upon recording. On this record, defendants have not identified any competent evidence creating a genuine dispute as to the Estate’s superior present title.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Do not say the deed to the Estate alone proves present title unless the record actually shows a legally effective delivery. Revise the paragraph to rely on the probate return orders and the executed deed, and only retain a title-passage sentence if plaintiff can cite record evidence of delivery.

challenges.opponent_argument: The probate order cited here is administrative, not possessory. An order authorizing the executrix to inventory, collect rents, pay taxes, make repairs, and insure the property does not itself say that the Estate was awarded exclusive present possession. The brief cites no authority for the leap from management powers to a superior right of possession, and the record excerpt does not contain such a decree.
challenges.why_it_matters: If the order is only an administration order, it cannot substitute for proof of the statutory right to possession.

record_sources.title: record-01-record
record_sources.quote: IT IS FURTHER ORDERED that the Executor has the power to manage the real properties in question ... which includes but is not limited to, inventorying said premises, collecting rents, paying all taxes and assessments, making repairs and insuring buildings/residences accordingly.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is a real limitation on the alternative possession theory. The cited probate order language in the brief looks administrative—inventorying, collecting rents, paying taxes, making repairs, insuring—and the authority cited in the record does not clearly say that such management powers alone confer present possessory rights. The brief tries to bridge that gap with Sed v. Mundy, but the source material supplied here does not fully supply the same proposition. A court could view this as enough only if title-transfer theory succeeds; standing alone, it is vulnerable.
challenges.suggested_response: The probate court did more than authorize routine administration: it ordered the Cedar Road property returned to the Estate, and then authorized the Estate to manage the premises, including inventorying the property, collecting rents, paying taxes and assessments, making repairs, and insuring the buildings. Those orders, together with the defendants’ deed conveying the Premises to the Estate, confirm that the Estate—not defendants—has the superior present right to possession.

record_sources.quote: You are being asked to leave for the following reason: you occupy the premises without color of title, and the Estate of Anthony Notarian has title and the right to possession; ... you were ordered to return title and possession of the real property to the Estate of Anthony Notarian by the Court of Common Pleas, Probate Division, Geauga County ... by Court Order on March 16, 2022, and subsequent orders.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is a legitimate summary-judgment objection if the only proof is the Estate's characterization of defendants as occupants without color of title. Ohio's FED statute turns on that statutory status, and the record excerpt here does not independently spell out why defendants lack color of title. That said, if the court accepts the probate order and deed as establishing superior title in the Estate, the color-of-title point becomes much easier for plaintiff. So this is not as strong as the title-transfer attack, but it is a real gap if the underlying title proof is not solid.
challenges.suggested_response: The record shows that defendants were ordered to return the Cedar Road property to the Estate and later executed a deed conveying the Premises to the Estate. They remain in possession only in defiance of those orders and without any competent evidence of present title in themselves. Under R.C. 1923.02(A)(5), defendants are occupiers without color of title, and the Estate, as the party with the right of possession, is entitled to restitution.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Tie the no-color-of-title point to the probate orders and the executed deed, rather than to plaintiff’s characterization alone. If the record does not independently prove the absence of color of title, say that the Estate’s title proof establishes that defendants cannot claim a superior possessory right.

attacks_proposed.argument: The Estate has not carried its summary-judgment burden on present title. The brief jumps from a probate order and the fact that defendants later executed a deed to the conclusion that title passed, but the supplied record excerpt does not show an effective delivery or any other fact establishing when title actually transferred. Under the title-issues authority, present possession turns on present record title; without competent evidence establishing that title passed, entitlement to possession is not established as a matter of law.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If title is not conclusively established, the court cannot grant possession judgment on summary judgment.

attacks_proposed.argument: The probate order cited here is administrative, not possessory. An order authorizing the executrix to inventory, collect rents, pay taxes, make repairs, and insure the property does not itself say that the Estate was awarded exclusive present possession. The brief cites no authority for the leap from management powers to a superior right of possession, and the record excerpt does not contain such a decree.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If the order is only an administration order, it cannot substitute for proof of the statutory right to possession.

attacks_proposed.argument: The Estate still must prove the statutory FED element that defendants are occupiers without color of title. The record excerpt shows only the Estate’s own characterization of defendants’ status and reliance on prior orders; it does not independently establish the absence of color of title. Ohio’s title-issues authority also recognizes that an occupant may assert ownership to defeat eviction. That leaves a genuine issue, not a summary-judgment record.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Without proof that defendants lack color of title, a writ of restitution is premature.

attacks_proposed.argument: The motion frames this as a pure Civ.R. 56 problem, but the movant’s own theory makes present title the predicate for possession. Because the record supplied here does not conclusively establish title transfer or eliminate defendants’ contrary possessory claim, the court is being asked to decide a disputed title-dependent possession issue as a matter of law. The general summary-judgment standard does not cure that evidentiary gap.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If the court sees a genuine title/possession dispute, partial summary judgment should be denied and the issue should proceed on a fuller record.

judge_assessments.assessment: This lands. Ohio authority cited by both sides makes present title central to the right of possession, and the record excerpt does not itself show the mechanics of delivery needed to make the deed effective. The brief does say defendants executed a deed on February 1, 2023 and cites Wayne/Gordon for the proposition that delivery passes title, but the contested point is whether this record actually establishes a legally effective delivery to the Estate rather than just an executed instrument. If the court is unconvinced on delivery, summary judgment on possession fails.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: Defendants executed a deed conveying the Premises back to the Estate on February 1, 2023; title passes upon proper execution and delivery regardless of recording; delivery of this deed to the probate court constitutes delivery of title.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The decisive missing piece is the actual deed/exhibit language and any evidence showing delivery, escrow, acceptance, or present intent to transfer title.

judge_assessments.assessment: This is a real limitation on the alternative possession theory. The cited probate order language in the brief looks administrative—inventorying, collecting rents, paying taxes, making repairs, insuring—and the authority cited in the record does not clearly say that such management powers alone confer present possessory rights. The brief tries to bridge that gap with Sed v. Mundy, but the source material supplied here does not fully supply the same proposition. A court could view this as enough only if title-transfer theory succeeds; standing alone, it is vulnerable.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: Judge Grendell entered orders giving the Estate power to manage the Cedar Road Property, including inventorying, collecting rents, paying taxes and assessments, making repairs, and insuring the premises; the brief says the Estate has the right to administer the Cedar Road Premises and cites Sed v. Mundy for a superior right to possession.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Would need the actual probate orders and the full Sed opinion to see whether administration authority was treated as a possessory right or merely an incidental power.

judge_assessments.assessment: This is a legitimate summary-judgment objection if the only proof is the Estate's characterization of defendants as occupants without color of title. Ohio's FED statute turns on that statutory status, and the record excerpt here does not independently spell out why defendants lack color of title. That said, if the court accepts the probate order and deed as establishing superior title in the Estate, the color-of-title point becomes much easier for plaintiff. So this is not as strong as the title-transfer attack, but it is a real gap if the underlying title proof is not solid.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: Defendants are living in the Premises; they refuse to remove their belongings or turn over possession; the Estate says defendants do not have a key to the Property; the brief says they are occupiers without color of title and in violation of court orders.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Would need the deed chain, any recorded conveyance, and the actual title/order exhibits to see whether defendants retained any colorable claim.

judge_assessments.assessment: This is just a repackaging of the title-transfer attack and does not add a separate defect. The brief already frames Civ.R. 56 and the FED standard; the real question is whether the underlying title and possession facts are established. A court would not likely treat this as an independent ground for denial beyond the specific title and possession objections already captured in a1 and a3.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief quotes Civ.R. 56(C), Temple, and Siegler and argues there is no genuine issue of material fact and that summary judgment procedures apply to FED actions.

judge_assessments.assessment: This attack misreads the brief. The motion does say the notice was served at the Premises, and the statute expressly allows service by leaving the notice at the premises sought to be evicted. On this record, the cited source supports that method, so the complaint that the brief omitted a permitted service method does not land. If the exhibit actually showed a different or defective method, that would be a different issue, but this attack as framed is not persuasive.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: Plaintiff served the defendants with an eviction notice on June 28, 2023; the notice was served at least three days before filing; plaintiff served the notice at the Premises; the notice included the mandated statutory language in bold lettering.

results.verdict: not yet persuasive on the central possession element
results.assessment: The brief has a workable structure and its best point is the straightforward reliance on the probate orders and the February 1, 2023 deed to argue superior possession. But as written it is exposed on the core issue: the record excerpt does not itself show an effective delivery or other competent proof that present title actually passed, so the title-based possession theory is vulnerable. It also overreads the probate orders, which look administrative rather than a clear award of exclusive present possession, and it does not independently establish that defendants are occupiers without color of title. Those are the fixes that matter most; the research did not settle away the delivery problem or the limited force of the probate orders standing alone.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is the best attack on the possession theory. Ohio FED relief turns on the complainant's present right to possession, and the brief itself relies on present title and on probate orders to establish it. Source support exists for the general proposition, but on this record the estate is asking the court to treat the probate proceedings and deed as conclusive without showing the actual title chain or preclusive effect in this case. If the probate orders are not legally dispositive, the motion loses its core element.
challenges.suggested_response: R.C. 1923.02(A)(5) permits forcible entry and detainer where the defendants are occupiers of the Premises without color of title and the complainant has the right of possession. That is the situation here. The Probate Court ordered the Premises returned to the Estate, the deed conveying the Premises to the Estate was executed, and Ohio law holds that title passes upon proper execution and delivery of a deed without regard to recordation. Defendants therefore have no present title superior to the Estate's, and the Estate has the right of possession as a matter of law.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Make the R.C. 1923.02(A)(5) element explicit: the Estate must show present title/right of possession, and defendants must have no superior color of title. Tie that element directly to the probate return order, the executed deed, and the title-pass rule from the authorities already cited.

challenges.opponent_argument: The probate court's management order is not the same thing as an adjudication of exclusive possession. The order quoted in the brief authorizes the Estate to inventory, collect rents, pay taxes, make repairs, and insure the property; those are administrative powers, not a ruling that the Estate may oust the occupants on summary judgment. Under the authorities the brief itself invokes, the relevant question is present ownership and the right of possession, not merely authority to manage estate property.
challenges.why_it_matters: If the management order is not treated as a possessory judgment, the motion's main bridge from probate administration to FED relief collapses.

results.assessment: The motion has a workable structure and it does cite the right statutory possession language, but as written it is vulnerable on the core issue of present right to possession. The biggest gap is that it treats the probate orders and deed as if they conclusively establish title and ejectment authority without fully showing the title chain or the legal effect of those orders in this case. The management order is especially weak as an independent basis for eviction because it reads as administrative authority, not a possessory adjudication. The deed point helps, but the record still needs clearer proof of valid execution, delivery, and any preclusive effect of the probate proceedings.

results.assessment: The motion reads coherently on the common-law premises-liability theory: Armstrong supports the invitee/open-and-obvious analysis, and Baker has a usable argument that Friese pleaded only that theory. The weak point is that the brief speaks too broadly about the missing handrail and about res judicata. The supplied materials say open-and-obvious does not defeat an R.C. 5321.04 negligence-per-se claim, and Chapter 1923 judgments do not automatically bar later non-eviction claims. Baker needs to tighten both points by showing the absence of any pleaded or supported statutory/code theory and by tying preclusion specifically to Civ.R. 13(A) and the prior damages action.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is a real summary-judgment attack, but it is not a clean one. The brief already gives Baker the same-transaction story: the injury came from the rented premises, Friese says his invitee status arose from the tenancy, and the prior suit sought eviction plus monetary damages. Ohio authorities cited in the brief are used to support compulsory counterclaims in tenant-injury cases. The opponent can press the point, but Baker has already answered it with her own cases.
challenges.suggested_response: Even apart from the open-and-obvious defense, Friese’s personal-injury claim arose from the same tenancy that was the subject of Baker’s prior municipal-court action. Baker’s complaint in that case sought both eviction and monetary damages for rent and property damage; Friese’s alleged stairway injury occurred while he was still occupying the apartment, and his own Complaint alleges that his status on the premises arose from that tenancy. Under Civ.R. 13(A), and the authorities cited above, Friese was required to assert that claim in the earlier action.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: If Baker keeps any preclusion argument, make the Civ.R. 13(A) nexus explicit and stop calling it pure res judicata. Tie the claim to the same tenancy and the prior action for eviction plus monetary damages, and say the injury claim should have been asserted there as a compulsory counterclaim.

record_sources.quote: Q. And how many times a day would you use them, on average? A. Three to four. ... Q. But you were aware of their condition? A. Yeah. ... A. There was no handrail.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is the standard factual attack on open and obvious, but it is thin on this record. Friese's daily use of the stairs, his admitted knowledge that there was no railing, and the brief's point that the stairwell was lit all support Baker's position. Friese's statement that he saw nothing unusual before leaving and later missed a step does not create much room to say the hazard was hidden. The court could still deny summary judgment on a close record, but this attack does not strongly move that needle.
challenges.suggested_response: Even assuming Friese was a business invitee, the summary-judgment record establishes that the condition of the stairway was open and obvious as a matter of law. Friese used the stairs three to four times each day for nearly four years, knew their condition, knew there was no handrail, and testified that the stairs were in the same condition when he fell. Under Armstrong and the open-and-obvious doctrine, Baker owed no duty to warn of a condition that was already known to Friese and readily observable. Friese’s statement that he saw nothing unusual does not create a genuine issue of material fact where the condition complained of was long familiar to him.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Tighten the open-and-obvious paragraph to rely on Friese’s admissions, and remove the unsupported concession that Baker does not dispute invitee status. Use an alternative framing if needed: even assuming invitee status, Baker owed no duty as to a hazard Friese already knew and used repeatedly.

That testimony does not eliminate factual disputes about the condition of the stairs or whether the lack of a handrail was the operative hazard.
challenges.why_it_matters: If the court must draw competing inferences from Friese's testimony, summary judgment is inappropriate.

results.assessment: The brief is strongest on the open-and-obvious issue: it has the better of the record-based points, and the challenges suggest Friese’s daily use of the stairs and knowledge of the missing handrail support Baker’s no-duty argument. The biggest weakness is the res judicata section, which is exposed because the prior municipal-court judgment appears to fall within the Chapter 1923 carveout and cannot, by itself, bar this suit. The compulsory-counterclaim theory is better than res judicata but still needs cleaner tying together of the same-transaction facts. The conflict in Friese’s fall testimony does not seem to create a meaningful summary-judgment problem for Baker.
